about.headline: Why use a GST calculator
paragraphs: GST shows up everywhere in a business's day-to-day — quoting a price to a customer, checking a supplier invoice, or working out what to enter on a bill. Doing the maths by hand for every slab is slow and easy to get wrong, especially when you're moving between rates like 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%.

This calculator works both ways. Enter a base amount to see the GST and total with tax added, or enter a final amount to see what the base price and tax were before GST was included. It's the same calculation Setu Dine runs automatically on every bill, available here as a free, standalone tool.

items.question: How do I calculate GST on an amount?
items.answer: Multiply the base amount by the GST rate and divide by 100 to get the GST amount, then add it to the base amount for the total. For example, ₹1,000 at 18% GST adds ₹180, for a total of ₹1,180.

items.question: How do I remove GST from a final price to find the base price?
items.answer: Divide the final amount by (1 + GST rate/100). For a final amount of ₹1,180 at 18% GST, the base price is ₹1,180 ÷ 1.18 = ₹1,000.

items.question: What are the common GST slabs in India?
items.answer: The most common GST slabs are 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%, though some goods and services fall outside these or are exempt. Always check the rate that applies to what you're billing.

items.question: Does Setu Dine calculate GST automatically?

items.question: How do I split GST into CGST and SGST?
items.answer: For a sale within your own state, the GST amount is divided equally: half is CGST and half is SGST. At 18%, that is 9% CGST and 9% SGST, so ₹1,800 of GST on a ₹10,000 bill becomes ₹900 each. The calculator shows the combined GST amount, so halve it for the two lines on your invoice. Sales to another state carry the whole amount as IGST.

items.question: Can I enter a GST rate that is not on the preset buttons?

items.question: What is the difference between a tax-inclusive and a tax-exclusive price?
items.answer: A tax-exclusive price is the base amount before GST, with tax added on top at billing. A tax-inclusive price already contains the GST. Use Add GST mode for a tax-exclusive price to find the total, and Remove GST mode for a tax-inclusive price to find the base and the tax inside it. The MRP printed on packaged goods is inclusive of all taxes.

guide.headline: Worked example: GST on a ₹10,000 invoice
paragraphs: Say a Pune agency bills a local client ₹10,000 for a service taxed at 18%. In the GST calculator's Add GST mode, enter 10000 as the amount and 18 as the rate. The GST amount is 10,000 × 18 ÷ 100 = ₹1,800, so the Total amount is ₹11,800. Because the client is in the same state, the invoice shows [CGST](/glossary/cgst) of ₹900 and [SGST](/glossary/sgst) of ₹900. If the same job were billed to a client in Bengaluru, the full ₹1,800 would be charged as [IGST](/glossary/igst).

Now the reverse. A customer paid ₹1,050 for a meal at a restaurant charging 5% GST and wants to know the tax in it. In Remove GST mode, enter 1050 and 5: Base amount = 1,050 ÷ 1.05 = ₹1,000 and GST amount = 1,050 − 1,000 = ₹50. Taking 5% of ₹1,050 (₹52.50) would overstate the tax, because the rate applies to the base price, not to the tax-inclusive total.

guide.headline: GST billing tips and common mistakes
items: Check the rate for your exact HSN or SAC code before billing. Since 22 September 2025 most goods and services fall under 5% or 18%, with 40% for a short list of sin and luxury goods.
The 12% and 28% preset buttons are mainly useful for checking older invoices; most items that sat in those slabs have moved to 5%, 18% or 40%.
Never remove GST by taking the rate off the total: ₹11,800 minus 18% gives ₹9,676, not the correct base of ₹10,000.
Say clearly on menus, price lists and quotations whether prices include GST, so customers are not surprised at billing.
If you are registered under the composition scheme, you cannot collect GST from customers, so the Add GST result does not belong on your bills.
Keep the GST amount from every purchase bill. A regular registered business can usually claim it as input tax credit, but composition dealers and restaurants billing at 5% without credit cannot.

about.headline: Why margin and markup both matter
paragraphs: Profit margin tells you what share of your selling price is actual profit — useful for checking whether a product or dish is genuinely worth selling at its current price. Markup tells you how much you've added on top of cost — useful when you're setting a price from scratch.

The two numbers look similar but aren't the same: a 50% markup on cost is only a 33% margin on the selling price. This calculator shows both together so you can sanity-check pricing decisions without mixing the two up.

items.question: What is the formula for profit margin?
items.answer: Profit margin % = (Selling Price − Cost Price) ÷ Selling Price × 100. It measures profit as a percentage of the selling price.

items.question: What's the difference between margin and markup?
items.answer: Margin is profit divided by selling price; markup is profit divided by cost price. They use the same profit figure but different denominators, so a given profit amount produces a higher markup % than margin %.

items.question: What's a good profit margin for a small business?
items.answer: It varies widely by industry — restaurants often run 10-15% net margin, while retail margins vary by category. Compare your margin against your own historical numbers and industry benchmarks rather than a single universal target.

items.question: Should I price based on margin or markup?
items.answer: Most businesses set prices using markup on cost, then check the resulting margin to confirm it meets their profit target. Using both avoids underpricing items that look fine by one measure but not the other.

items.question: Should I include GST when calculating profit margin?
items.answer: If you are GST-registered under the regular scheme and claim input tax credit, leave GST out of both prices. The GST you collect belongs to the government, and the GST you paid on purchases comes back as credit. If you are under the composition scheme or not registered, you cannot claim that credit, so include the GST you paid in your cost price; composition tax on your turnover also comes out of your margin.

items.question: What is the difference between gross margin and net margin?
items.answer: Gross margin is what is left from sales after the direct cost of the goods, which is closest to what this calculator shows for a single item. Net margin is what is left after every expense, including rent, salaries, electricity, interest and tax. A shop can have a healthy 30% gross margin and still make a loss if its overheads are high.

items.question: Can profit margin be more than 100%?
items.answer: No. Profit can never be larger than the selling price, so margin stays below 100% and reaches it only if the cost is zero. Markup has no ceiling. Buying at ₹50 and selling at ₹200 is a 300% markup but a 75% margin. For the same item, the markup figure is always the higher of the two, so make sure you know which one a supplier or salesperson is quoting.

items.question: How do I find the selling price for a target margin?
items.answer: Divide the cost by one minus the target margin. For a ₹600 cost and a 40% margin, that is 600 ÷ 0.60 = ₹1,000. You can confirm it here by entering ₹600 as the cost price and ₹1,000 as the selling price; the calculator will show a ₹400 profit, a 40% margin and a 66.7% markup.

guide.headline: Worked example: margin on a ₹999 kurta
paragraphs: A clothing shop buys a kurta for ₹640 including freight and sells it for ₹999 before GST. Enter both figures in the profit margin calculator and it shows a profit of ₹359, a profit margin of 35.9% (359 ÷ 999 × 100) and a markup of 56.1% (359 ÷ 640 × 100). Put another way, about 36 paise of every rupee the customer pays is profit before rent, salaries and other overheads.

At the end-of-season sale the price drops to ₹849. Profit falls to ₹209, margin to 24.6% and markup to 32.7%. A 15% price cut has taken away about 42% of the profit on each kurta, so the shop must sell about 1.7 kurtas at the sale price to earn what one earned at full price. That is the real cost of a [markdown](/glossary/markdown).

guide.headline: Common profit margin mistakes
items: Using the printed MRP as the selling price. MRP includes GST and you may sell below it, so enter what customers actually pay, net of tax.
Leaving freight, loading, packing or wastage out of the cost price, which makes every margin look better than it is.
Forgetting returns, damaged pieces and free samples. Their cost has to be recovered from the units you do sell, so allow for it in your price.
Using one average margin for the whole shop. High- and low-margin items blend together, so check top sellers one by one.
Not rechecking after a supplier price rise. If cost goes from ₹100 to ₹120 on an item sold at ₹150, margin drops from 33.3% to 20%.

about.headline: Pricing from cost upward
paragraphs: Cost-plus pricing — taking your cost and adding a fixed markup — is the simplest way to price a new product or menu item. The hard part is doing it consistently across dozens of SKUs or dishes without a calculator open in another tab for every one.

This tool flips the usual margin question around: instead of checking the margin on a price you've already picked, you tell it the markup you want and it gives you the price to charge, along with the profit per unit at that price.

items.question: What is the markup formula?
items.answer: Selling Price = Cost Price × (1 + Markup % ÷ 100). For example, a ₹100 cost item with a 40% markup sells at ₹140.

items.question: Is a 50% markup the same as a 50% margin?
items.answer: No. A 50% markup on a ₹100 cost gives a ₹150 selling price, which works out to a 33.3% margin, not 50%. Markup and margin are calculated on different bases.

items.question: What markup should I use for retail products?
items.answer: It depends on the category, competition and how much value-add or service comes with the product. Many retailers start in the 30-50% markup range and adjust based on what sells and what the market will bear.

items.question: Can I use this for restaurant menu pricing too?
items.answer: Yes — enter your plate cost as the cost price and your target markup to get a starting menu price, then sanity-check it against the food cost percentage calculator.

items.question: Does the selling price from the markup calculator include GST?
items.answer: No. The calculator adds your markup to the cost you enter and nothing else, so the result is the price before tax. If you are GST-registered and claim input tax credit, enter your cost without GST, then add GST at your item's rate on top of the calculated price. If you show tax-inclusive prices on a menu or shelf label, the final price will be higher than the figure shown here.

items.question: Can a markup be more than 100%?
items.answer: Yes. A 100% markup doubles the cost, and anything above that is common for low-cost items such as accessories, beverages or packaged snacks. For example, a 150% markup on a ₹200 cost gives a ₹500 selling price and a ₹300 profit, which the calculator shows as a 60% resulting margin.

items.question: What is the difference between markup and MRP?
items.answer: MRP, the maximum retail price, is the highest price at which a packaged product may be sold. The manufacturer, packer or importer prints it on the pack, and it includes all taxes. Markup is what you add on top of your own cost. For packaged goods, the MRP caps how much markup you can take; for loose items, services or dishes there is no MRP, so your markup and the market set the price.

items.question: Can I use the markup calculator in a currency other than rupees?
items.answer: Yes. The calculator follows the currency saved in Setu's free Business Profile tool. Choose your currency there, fill in your business name and save, and the cost field and results on this page switch to that currency's symbol instead of the rupee. The markup arithmetic is the same in any currency.

guide.headline: Markup formula
guide.text: Selling price = Cost price × (1 + Markup % ÷ 100). Profit per unit = Selling price − Cost price. Resulting margin % = Profit per unit ÷ Selling price × 100.

guide.headline: How to use the markup calculator
steps: Enter the cost price of one unit, including freight and packing, or the plate cost of a dish.
Enter your target markup %.
Read the selling price, the profit per unit and the resulting margin %.
Round the selling price to a price point that suits your shelf or menu, then check the rounded price in the profit margin calculator.

guide.headline: Worked example: pricing kaju katli at a 65% markup
paragraphs: A sweet shop works out that one kilo of kaju katli costs ₹720 to make, counting cashews, sugar, varq, gas, labour and the box. With a 65% markup, the markup calculator gives a selling price of ₹1,188 (720 × 1.65), a profit of ₹468 per kilo and a resulting margin of 39.4% (468 ÷ 1,188 × 100). On the price board the shop might round that to ₹1,190 or ₹1,200 a kilo.

Suppose the owner thinks in margin instead and wants 30%. The markup needed is 30 ÷ (100 − 30) × 100 = 42.86%. Entering 42.86% gives a selling price of ₹1,028.59 and a profit of ₹308.59 per kilo, and the resulting margin shows 30%. Converting the target margin first stops you from pricing at a 30% markup and ending up with only a 23% margin. This is the core of [cost-plus pricing](/glossary/cost-plus-pricing).

guide.headline: Markup tips before you print the price
items: Build the full landed cost first: purchase price, freight, loading, packing and expected breakage or wastage.
Use a higher markup on slow-moving, fragile or perishable items to cover the stock that never sells.
Check what is left after offers and platform commission. A 40% markup cut by a 20% discount leaves only about a 10.7% margin.
Let competitors' prices set your ceiling. Markup gives you a floor based on cost; what customers will pay decides how far above it you can go.
When a supplier raises prices, re-apply the same markup % to the new cost. Adding only the rupee increase quietly lowers your margin.

hero.headline: Break-Even Point Calculator

about.headline: Know your number before the month starts
paragraphs: Your break-even point is the level of sales where revenue exactly covers your costs — sell less and you're in a loss, sell more and every extra unit is pure contribution to profit. It's one of the most useful numbers in a business because it turns rent, salaries and other fixed costs into a single, concrete sales target.

Enter your monthly fixed costs (rent, salaries, subscriptions), your variable cost per unit (ingredients, packaging, per-order costs) and your selling price, and this calculator works out the units and revenue you need to hit before you're in profit.

items.question: What is the break-even point formula?
items.answer: Break-even units = Fixed Costs ÷ (Selling Price per unit − Variable Cost per unit). Multiply the result by the selling price to get break-even revenue.

items.question: What counts as a fixed cost vs a variable cost?
items.answer: Fixed costs stay roughly the same regardless of sales volume — rent, salaries, software subscriptions. Variable costs scale with each unit sold — ingredients, packaging, payment gateway fees per order.

items.question: Why does break-even matter for a new restaurant or store?
items.answer: It converts your overheads into a daily or monthly sales target, which makes it much easier to judge whether a location, menu price or staffing level is realistic before you commit to it.

items.question: What is contribution margin?
items.answer: Contribution margin is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit — the amount each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs. A higher contribution margin means you break even with fewer units sold.

items.question: Why does the break-even calculator say there is no break-even point?
items.answer: This happens when the selling price per unit is equal to or lower than the variable cost per unit. Each sale then adds nothing, or loses money, before fixed costs are even counted, so no sales volume can cover rent and salaries. The calculator shows a warning instead of results. Raise the price or cut the variable cost, and check that you have not compared a GST-inclusive cost with a pre-GST price.

items.question: How do I work out my margin of safety from the break-even point?
items.answer: Margin of safety is how far your actual sales sit above break-even. Subtract break-even revenue from your current monthly sales, then divide by current sales for a percentage. If you sell ₹3,60,000 a month and break even at ₹3,00,000, your margin of safety is ₹60,000, or about 16.7%. The bigger this cushion, the better you can absorb a slow month or a cost increase.

items.question: Should I include GST in the selling price for break-even analysis?
items.answer: If you are a regular GST-registered business, no. The GST you collect is passed on to the government, so enter the selling price before tax, and enter purchase costs net of any input tax credit you can claim. Under the composition scheme you cannot collect GST from customers or claim input tax credit, so treat the tax you pay on turnover as a variable cost and enter purchase costs including GST.

items.question: Is the break-even calculator free, and does it save my numbers?
items.answer: Yes, it is free to use with no sign-up, and the results update as you type. It does not save your inputs: reloading the page brings back the sample figures. Note down your fixed costs, variable cost and selling price, or keep them in a spreadsheet, so you can re-run the calculation quickly when costs or prices change.

guide.headline: Break-even point formula
guide.text: Contribution per unit = Selling price per unit − Variable cost per unit. Contribution margin % = Contribution per unit ÷ Selling price per unit × 100. Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Break-even revenue = Break-even units × Selling price per unit. If the selling price is not higher than the variable cost, there is **no break-even point** and the calculator shows a warning instead of results.

guide.headline: How to use the break-even calculator
steps: Add up the costs you pay every month whatever your sales, such as rent, staff salaries, fixed electricity charges and software subscriptions, and enter the total in Fixed costs (per month).
Decide what one unit means for your business: a product, a plate or an average bill. Use that same unit for the next two fields.
Enter the Variable cost per unit: everything you spend each time you sell one unit, such as ingredients, packaging, delivery app commission and card payment charges.
Enter the Selling price per unit as the amount you actually receive, after any regular discount and before GST.
Read Break-even units, Break-even revenue and Contribution margin. They update as you type.
Divide the break-even units or revenue by the number of days you are open to get a daily sales target.

guide.headline: Worked example: break-even for a café with ₹1,80,000 monthly costs
paragraphs: A café pays ₹70,000 rent, ₹90,000 in salaries and about ₹20,000 for electricity, internet and software each month, so its [fixed costs](/glossary/fixed-cost) are ₹1,80,000. Its average bill is ₹400, and the ingredients, packaging and payment charges behind that bill come to ₹160. Each bill therefore contributes ₹400 − ₹160 = ₹240, a contribution margin of 60%. The break-even calculator divides ₹1,80,000 by ₹240 and shows 750 bills, or ₹3,00,000 in sales (750 × ₹400). Open 30 days a month, that is 25 bills or ₹10,000 of sales a day.

Now suppose milk and coffee prices push the variable cost to ₹200 per bill while menu prices stay the same. Contribution drops to ₹200, and break-even rises to ₹1,80,000 ÷ ₹200 = 900 bills, or ₹3,60,000 in sales. A ₹40 rise in cost per bill means 150 more bills every month, 20% more, just to reach zero profit. Whenever a supplier raises rates, recheck your [contribution margin](/glossary/contribution-margin) before deciding whether menu prices need to move.

guide.headline: Break-even mistakes to avoid
items: Leaving out your own salary. If you work full time in the business, add a fair monthly drawing to fixed costs, or break-even will look easier than it is.
Counting only ingredients as variable costs. Delivery app commission, packaging, card payment charges (MDR) and per-order staff incentives also rise with every sale.
Ignoring loan repayments. The principal part of an EMI is not an expense in your P&L, but it still needs cash, so add EMIs to fixed costs if you want a cash break-even figure.
Reading the units as exact. Break-even units are rounded to the nearest whole number on screen; when planning, round any fraction up, since 642.3 bills shows as 642 but means you need 643.
Planning around an average month. Seasonal businesses should check break-even against their slowest months, not the yearly average.
Calculating once and forgetting it. Re-run the numbers whenever rent, salaries, supplier rates or menu prices change.

about.headline: The single number every menu price should pass

items.question: How do you calculate food cost percentage?
items.answer: Food Cost % = (Ingredient Cost ÷ Menu Selling Price) × 100. A dish costing ₹70 in ingredients sold at ₹280 has a food cost of 25%.

items.question: What is a good food cost percentage for a restaurant?
items.answer: Most full-service and quick-service restaurants target 28-35% food cost, but high-end ingredients, beverages and bakery items can run lower or higher and still be profitable once labour and overhead are factored in.

items.question: Why is my food cost percentage higher than expected?
items.answer: Common causes are portion sizes drifting larger over time, ingredient price increases that prices haven't caught up to, wastage in the kitchen, or recipes that were never costed properly to begin with.

items.question: Does this account for labour cost?
items.answer: No — this calculator covers raw ingredient (food) cost only. Labour, packaging and overhead should be tracked separately alongside food cost when deciding final menu prices.

items.question: Should I enter the menu price with or without GST?
items.answer: Enter the price before GST. The tax on a bill goes to the government, so it is not part of what the dish earns you. If your menu prices include GST, divide by 1.05 for the 5% rate most restaurants charge: a dish listed at ₹315 is ₹300 before tax. items.question: What is the difference between theoretical and actual food cost?
items.answer: Theoretical food cost is what this calculator shows: the recipe cost of a dish against its price, assuming exact portions and no waste. Actual food cost covers a whole period: (opening stock + purchases − closing stock) ÷ food sales × 100. If your actual figure runs well above the theoretical one, the gap is going on wastage, over-portioning, staff meals or missing stock.

items.question: How is food cost percentage related to gross margin on a dish?
items.answer: The two always add up to 100% of the menu price. A dish with a 30% food cost has a 70% gross margin, which the calculator shows in rupees as gross profit per dish, for example ₹70 on a ₹100 dish. Because only ingredients are counted, rent, salaries, gas and electricity still have to be paid out of that gross profit before the dish makes a net profit.

items.question: Can I use this calculator for dishes sold on Zomato or Swiggy?

Multiply each quantity by your latest purchase price to get each ingredient's cost, then add them up. The Recipe Costing Calculator can total the ingredient costs for you and divide a batch by its number of servings.
Enter the total in Ingredient cost per dish.
Enter the Menu selling price of that dish, before GST.
Read Food cost % and Gross profit per dish. A note below the results flags dishes above 35%.
Repeat for each dish on the menu, and again whenever a supplier changes prices.

guide.headline: Worked example: food cost for a ₹320 paneer dish
paragraphs: A portion of paneer butter masala uses 150 g of paneer at ₹400 per kg (₹60), ₹22 of butter, cream and cashew, and ₹14 of tomato, onion, oil and spices, for a total [plate cost](/glossary/plate-cost) of ₹96. Entered with a menu price of ₹320, the food cost calculator shows a food cost percentage of 30% (₹96 ÷ ₹320 × 100) and a gross profit of ₹224 per dish, inside the range most kitchens aim for.

A chicken biryani priced at ₹280 with ₹110 of ingredients comes out at 39.3%, and the calculator flags it as above range. To bring it to 32%, either raise the price to about ₹345 (₹110 ÷ 0.32 = ₹343.75, rounded up), which gives 31.9%, or keep ₹280 and bring the ingredient cost down to ₹89.60 (₹280 × 0.32), for example by adjusting the chicken portion or the [yield](/glossary/yield-percentage) you get from each kilo bought.

guide.headline: Food costing mistakes to avoid
items: Leaving out small items. Oil, ghee, masalas, garnish, chutneys and complimentary sides all belong in the plate cost.
Ignoring yield. Bone-in chicken, unpeeled onions and leafy greens give less usable weight than you buy, so cost the usable quantity.
Costing at old prices. Use the rate on your latest supplier bill, not the rate from when the menu was set.
Judging by percentage alone. A ₹600 dish at 40% food cost earns ₹360 a plate, more than a ₹200 dish at 25%, which earns ₹150.
Costing a thali or combo by its main item only. Add every component, including rice, roti, dal, raita, papad and pickle, and enter the total against the combo price.

It's also handy for checking a supplier's discount offer on a bulk order, or for quickly answering a customer's "how much is that after the discount" question without reaching for a phone calculator.

items.question: How do I calculate a discounted price?
items.answer: Discount Amount = Original Price × Discount % ÷ 100. Final Price = Original Price − Discount Amount. A ₹500 item at 20% off saves ₹100, for a final price of ₹400.

items.question: How does running a discount affect my profit margin?
items.answer: A discount reduces your selling price but not your cost, so it eats directly into margin. Check the profit margin calculator on the discounted price before running a promotion to make sure it's still worth selling at.

items.question: Can I stack two discounts together?
items.answer: Apply them one after another rather than adding the percentages — a 20% discount followed by a further 10% off is not a 30% total discount. Run the first discount through the calculator, then run the result through again for the second discount.

items.question: Can Setu Dine apply discounts and coupons automatically at billing?
items.answer: Yes. Setu Dine supports configurable coupons and discounts that apply automatically at the bill, so staff don't need to calculate offers manually at the counter.

items.question: How do I calculate the discount percentage from the original and sale price?
items.answer: Subtract the sale price from the original price, divide by the original price and multiply by 100. An item marked down from ₹2,000 to ₹1,500 carries a discount of ₹500 ÷ ₹2,000 × 100 = 25%. This calculator works forward from a percentage, so enter the figure you get to confirm the final price matches what you planned.

items.question: Is GST calculated before or after the discount?
items.answer: When the discount is given at or before the time of sale and shown on the tax invoice, GST is charged on the discounted price. A ₹1,000 item with 10% off and 18% GST is billed at ₹900 plus ₹162 GST, a total of ₹1,062. Discounts given after the sale, such as year-end supplier rebates, follow stricter conditions, so check the treatment with your CA/CPA.

items.question: What is the difference between a discount and a markdown?
items.answer: A discount is usually a temporary or conditional reduction, such as a festive offer, coupon or bulk-order rate, after which the price returns to normal. A markdown is a permanent cut to the selling price, often used to clear slow-moving or end-of-season stock. Both reduce your margin in the same way, and this calculator works out the new price for either.

items.question: Can I use the discount calculator on my phone?
items.answer: Yes. The page works in any mobile browser with nothing to install, and on a small screen the two fields and the results stack in a single column. Each field brings up a numeric keypad, and You save and Final price update as you type, so there is no button to press. Bookmark the page so it is one tap away during a sale.

guide.headline: Discount formula
guide.text: Discount amount (You save) = Original price × Discount % ÷ 100. Final price = Original price − Discount amount. Put together, Final price = Original price × (100 − Discount %) ÷ 100.

guide.headline: How to use the discount calculator
steps: Enter the Original price: the MRP, list price or menu price before the offer.
Enter the Discount as a percentage, for example 15 for 15% off. Decimals such as 12.5 work too.
Read You save, the rupee value of the discount on that item or bill.
Read Final price, the amount the customer pays after the discount.

guide.headline: Worked example: 25% off a ₹1,800 shirt
paragraphs: A clothing shop lists a shirt at ₹1,800 before GST and plans a 25% festive [promotional discount](/glossary/promotional-discount). The discount calculator shows You save ₹450 (₹1,800 × 25 ÷ 100) and a Final price of ₹1,350. The shirt costs the shop ₹1,080, so profit per shirt falls from ₹720 to ₹270, a drop of 62.5%. To earn the same total profit as before, the sale has to move about 2.7 times as many shirts (₹720 ÷ ₹270 = 2.67).

Multi-buy offers can be compared the same way. Buy 2, get 1 free on ₹600 items means the customer pays ₹1,200 for three pieces, or ₹400 each. Enter ₹600 and 33.33% and the calculator returns a final price of ₹400.02, the 2 paise being rounding, so the offer equals a one-third discount on every piece. That is deeper than 25% off, though it also moves three pieces per customer instead of one.

guide.headline: Before you announce a discount
items: Check the final price still covers your cost price plus per-sale costs such as packaging, delivery commission and card charges.
Convert flat offers to a percentage to compare them: ₹100 off is 25% on a ₹400 bill but only 10% on a ₹1,000 bill.
For packaged goods, quote the discount from the printed MRP. You can sell below MRP, never above it.
Set an end date or a minimum bill value so a promotion does not quietly become your regular price.
After the offer, compare units sold with the extra volume you needed. If sales did not rise enough to cover the lost margin, change the offer before repeating it.

about.headline: Know the monthly number before you sign
paragraphs: Whether it's a working capital loan, equipment financing or a line of credit to fund a new outlet, the EMI is the number that actually shows up against your cash flow every month. Comparing loan offers by interest rate alone can be misleading once tenure and processing costs are factored in.

Enter the loan amount, annual interest rate and tenure to get the EMI using the standard reducing-balance formula, along with the total interest you'll pay over the life of the loan — useful for comparing two offers side by side.

items.question: What is the EMI formula?
items.answer: EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100), and n is the number of monthly instalments.

items.question: Does this include processing fees or other charges?
items.answer: No — this calculates EMI based on principal, interest rate and tenure only. Add any processing fees or charges separately when comparing the true cost of different loan offers.

items.question: Is the interest rate I should enter the same as the rate the bank quotes?
items.answer: Use the annual interest rate as quoted by the lender. If a lender quotes a flat rate instead of a reducing-balance rate, the actual EMI will differ from what this calculator shows, since flat-rate loans charge interest on the full principal throughout the tenure.

items.question: How does a shorter tenure affect total interest?
items.answer: A shorter tenure means a higher EMI but significantly less total interest paid, since less time passes with interest accruing on the outstanding balance. A longer tenure lowers the EMI but increases total interest paid over the loan.

items.question: Can I use this EMI calculator for a home loan, car loan or personal loan?
items.answer: Yes, as long as the loan is repaid in equal monthly instalments on a reducing balance, which is how most bank home, car, personal and business loans in India work. The maths does not change with the loan type. It will not match loans that charge a flat rate, use step-up or balloon repayments, or start with an interest-only period, because those do not follow equal EMIs.

items.question: What happens if I enter 0% interest?
items.answer: The calculator divides the loan amount by the number of months, so a ₹6,00,000 interest-free loan over 24 months shows an EMI of ₹25,000 and total interest of zero. This is useful for an interest-free loan from a partner or family member. For a no-cost EMI offer on a purchase, read the invoice closely, since the interest is often recovered through a discount you do not get or a processing fee.

items.question: Does the calculator show a month-by-month amortisation schedule?
items.answer: No. It shows the monthly EMI, total interest and total payment for the whole loan. Inside each EMI the interest share is largest at the start and falls every month as the balance reduces, while the principal share grows. For the exact split of every instalment, ask your lender for the amortisation schedule, which banks usually provide with the sanction letter or on request.

items.question: Does the loan EMI calculator save what I enter?
items.answer: No. The figures you type are worked out in your browser and are not saved or sent anywhere, so they reset to the sample values when you reload the page. Note down the EMI and total interest for each offer if you want to compare them later. The calculator works the same on a phone, with the fields stacking in a single column.

guide.headline: Loan EMI formula
guide.text: Monthly rate r = Annual interest rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100, and n = tenure in months (years × 12). EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where P is the loan amount. Total payment = EMI × n. Total interest = Total payment − P. At 0% interest the calculator simply divides: EMI = P ÷ n. This is the [reducing-balance](/glossary/reducing-balance-interest) method, so each month's interest is charged only on the principal still outstanding.

guide.headline: How to use the Business Loan EMI Calculator
steps: Enter the amount you plan to borrow in the Loan amount field.
Enter the Annual interest rate from the lender's offer, as a reducing-balance rate.
Type the Tenure, then choose Months or Years below the field.
Read the Monthly EMI, Total interest and Total payment, which update as you type.
To compare two offers, change one input at a time, such as the tenure or the rate, and note the totals for each.

guide.headline: Worked example: EMI on a ₹10 lakh loan at 14%
paragraphs: Say you borrow ₹10,00,000 at 14% a year to fit out a second outlet. The monthly rate is 14 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = 0.011667. Over 36 months the loan EMI calculator gives an [EMI](/glossary/emi) of **₹34,177.63**, a total payment of ₹12,30,394.67 and total interest of ₹2,30,394.67. Stretch the same loan to 60 months and the EMI drops to ₹23,268.25, which is ₹10,909.38 less every month, but total interest rises to ₹3,96,095.05, or ₹1,65,700.38 more over the life of the loan.

Now compare two 36-month offers on the same ₹10 lakh. Offer A is 13% with a ₹20,000 processing fee; Offer B is 14% with no fee. At 13% the EMI is ₹33,693.95 and total interest is ₹2,12,982.27. Add the fee and Offer A's cost of borrowing comes to ₹2,32,982.27, which is ₹2,587.60 more than Offer B's ₹2,30,394.67. The lower rate is not the cheaper loan here, so add every fee to the calculator's total interest before you choose.

guide.headline: Checks before you take the loan
items: Fit the EMI into your slowest month, not your average month, after rent, salaries and supplier payments are covered.
Ask whether the first EMI includes broken-period interest for the days between disbursal and the first due date; the calculator assumes equal instalments from the first month.
Check the prepayment and foreclosure charges in the sanction letter if you expect to close the loan early from festive-season or year-end cash.
On a floating-rate loan, rerun the numbers at a rate 1 to 2 points higher, since lenders often extend the tenure rather than raise the EMI when rates go up.
Interest on a loan used for the business is generally a deductible expense, but the principal part of each EMI is not, so ask your CA/CPA to split the EMIs correctly in your books.

about.headline: The number behind a busy-looking dining room
paragraphs: Table turnover rate tells you how many times, on average, each table was used during a service period. It's a direct measure of how efficiently your floor is converting seats into covers — and during peak hours, it matters as much as footfall does.

Enter the total covers served, the number of tables you have, and the length of the service period, and this calculator works out your turnover rate and the average time each table was occupied per turn — useful for spotting whether slow turns are capping your revenue on busy nights.

items.question: How is table turnover rate calculated?
items.answer: Table Turnover Rate = Total Covers Served ÷ Number of Tables. If 120 covers were served across 20 tables during a service, the turnover rate is 6 — each table was used 6 times on average.

items.question: What is a good table turnover rate for a restaurant?
items.answer: It depends heavily on format — quick-service and casual dining aim for higher turnover (multiple turns per service), while fine dining intentionally runs lower turnover with longer dwell times and higher spend per cover. Compare against your own format and past performance.

items.question: How do I improve table turnover without rushing customers?
items.answer: Faster kitchen ticket times, efficient billing and payment, and staff trained to read natural pauses in a table's meal (rather than imposing a time limit) typically improve turnover more sustainably than rushing guests.

items.question: Can Setu Dine track table status in real time?
items.answer: Yes. Setu Dine shows live table status — open, occupied, billed — across your floor, so staff always know which tables are free without walking the room to check.

items.question: How do I calculate seat turnover instead of table turnover?
items.answer: Enter the number of seats in the Number of tables field and the number of guests in Covers served. The calculator divides the guests by the seats, so 120 guests across 60 seats over a 4-hour service gives a seat turnover of 2x and an average of 120 minutes per seat. This is useful when your floor mixes two-, four- and six-seat tables.

items.question: Why does the average turn time look longer than guests actually stay?
items.answer: The calculator spreads the whole service length across the turns, so minutes when a table sat empty, waited to be cleared or was held for a booking all count. On a quiet weeknight that can make a 50-minute meal look like a 90-minute turn. For a cleaner figure, measure only your busy window, when tables are reseated soon after guests leave.

items.question: Can I work out lunch and dinner table turnover separately?
items.answer: Yes, and it usually tells you more than a whole-day figure. Run the calculator once for lunch with lunch parties and lunch hours, for example 30 parties, 15 tables and 3 hours (2x, 90 minutes), and again for dinner with its own numbers. Comparing the two shows which service has spare table capacity and which one is genuinely full.

items.question: Does a higher table turnover rate always mean more revenue?
items.answer: No. Revenue depends on both turns and spend per party. Across 15 tables, 4 turns at an average bill of ₹1,200 brings in 60 × ₹1,200 = ₹72,000, while 3 turns at ₹1,800 brings in 45 × ₹1,800 = ₹81,000. Track your average bill alongside turnover so that faster turns do not come from smaller orders.

cta.headline: See every table's status, live
cta.subtext: Setu Dine tracks table status in real time, so your floor staff always know what's free.

guide.headline: Table turnover formula
guide.text: [Table turnover rate](/glossary/table-turnover-rate) = Covers served ÷ Number of tables. Average turn time (minutes) = Service length in hours × 60 ÷ Table turnover rate. The turn time assumes tables were in use for the whole service, so it includes minutes a table sat empty or was being reset between parties.

guide.headline: How to use the table turnover rate calculator
steps: Pick one service period, such as weekday lunch or Saturday dinner.
Enter Covers served for that period. Use the number of parties seated (bills) for true table turns, or the number of guests for covers per table.
Enter Number of tables that were open during the period, leaving out any section you closed.
Enter Service length in hours. Decimals work, so 7 pm to 10:30 pm is 3.5.
Read Table turnover rate (shown as 3x, 6x and so on) and Avg. turn time in minutes.

guide.headline: Worked example: Friday dinner at a 15-table restaurant
paragraphs: A 15-table restaurant serves dinner from 7 pm to 11 pm and seats 45 parties. Enter 45 in Covers served, 15 in Number of tables and 4 in Service length. The table turnover rate calculator shows 45 ÷ 15 = 3x and an average turn time of 4 × 60 ÷ 3 = 80 minutes. If you enter the 126 guests in those parties instead, it shows 8.4x and 29 minutes, which is [covers](/glossary/covers) per table, not the number of times a table was reset.

Now test a faster service. Enter 60 parties and the result becomes 4x with a 60-minute average turn. With an average bill of ₹1,800 per party, those 15 extra parties are worth 15 × ₹1,800 = ₹27,000 in one night, but only if guests are waiting for tables. If the floor is full and people are queuing at the door, that 20-minute gap is worth working on. On a half-empty night, turn time is not what limits sales.

guide.headline: Table turnover tips and common mistakes
items: Count only tables that were open. If you closed a section or held tables for a late booking, leave them out.
Measure the peak window on its own, such as 8 pm to 10 pm. A whole-evening figure hides the hours when tables actually run short.
Compare like with like, such as this Saturday dinner against last Saturday, not a Saturday against a Tuesday.
Take parties seated per service from your billing system so you are not counting from memory.
Watch your table size mix. If most parties are couples seated at four-seat tables, adding two-seat tables may raise turns more than faster service would.

This calculator gives a quick estimate of monthly take-home pay from an annual CTC figure, using typical PF and professional tax assumptions. Actual numbers depend on your specific salary structure (basic, HRA, allowances) and company policy, so treat this as a planning estimate rather than a payslip.

items.question: What is the difference between CTC and take-home salary?
items.answer: CTC is the total cost an employer bears for an employee, including basic pay, allowances, employer's PF contribution and other benefits. Take-home salary is what actually gets paid into the employee's bank account each month, after deductions like employee PF contribution, professional tax and income tax (if applicable).

items.question: Why is my take-home salary lower than CTC divided by 12?
items.answer: Because CTC includes employer contributions (like employer PF) that never reach the employee's bank account, and deductions like employee PF, professional tax and TDS are subtracted from gross pay before it's disbursed.

items.question: Is this calculator accurate for my exact salary slip?
items.answer: It's a planning estimate based on typical assumptions for PF and professional tax. Your actual take-home pay depends on your specific salary structure, state, and any additional deductions like income tax TDS, so use your company's payslip or HR for the exact figure.

items.question: Does this include income tax deduction?
items.answer: No — this calculator estimates deductions for PF and professional tax only. For an estimate that includes income tax, use the income tax calculator alongside this tool.

items.question: How is PF calculated in this take-home salary calculator?
items.answer: It takes 12% of your basic salary twice: once as the employer's contribution, which is part of CTC but never reaches your bank account, and once as your own contribution, deducted from gross pay. It applies 12% to the full basic with no wage ceiling, so if your employer limits PF to the statutory wage ceiling, your real take-home will be a little higher.

items.question: What basic salary percentage should I enter?
items.answer: Use the figure from your offer letter or payslip: monthly basic divided by monthly CTC, times 100. Many Indian companies set basic at around 40% to 50% of CTC, and the calculator starts at 40%. A higher basic means more PF deducted and lower monthly take-home, but larger PF savings and a bigger gratuity later.

items.question: How much professional tax should I enter?
items.answer: Enter the monthly amount your state deducts from salary. Professional tax is a state levy capped at ₹2,500 a year, and ₹200 a month is a common figure where it applies; the calculator starts at ₹200. Some states, including Delhi, do not charge it, so enter 0 there. Your payslip shows the exact deduction.

items.question: Can an employer use this calculator to plan a salary offer?
items.answer: Yes. Enter the annual CTC you plan to offer and the basic percentage in your salary structure to see what the employee will receive each month. Employer PF is inside the CTC figure, so CTC is your full yearly cost for the role before any bonus or insurance you add on top. Compare that cost with the sales the role will support.

guide.headline: Take-home salary formula
guide.text: Monthly CTC = Annual CTC ÷ 12. Basic = Monthly CTC × Basic % ÷ 100. Employer PF = Employee PF = Basic × 12%. Gross monthly salary = Monthly CTC − Employer PF. Monthly take-home = Gross monthly salary − Employee PF − Professional tax. Annual take-home = Monthly take-home × 12.

guide.headline: How to use the take-home salary calculator
steps: Enter your annual CTC from the offer letter or appointment letter.
Enter basic salary as a percentage of CTC. If your payslip shows basic as a monthly amount, divide it by monthly CTC and multiply by 100.
Enter the monthly professional tax your state deducts, or 0 if your state does not levy it.
Read the monthly take-home, the employee PF deducted each month and the annual take-home.
Change the basic percentage to see how a different salary structure moves your in-hand pay.

guide.headline: Worked example: ₹6 lakh CTC with 40% basic
paragraphs: A store supervisor is offered a CTC of ₹6,00,000 with basic set at 40% and ₹200 a month of [professional tax](/glossary/professional-tax). In the take-home salary calculator, monthly CTC is ₹6,00,000 ÷ 12 = ₹50,000, so basic is ₹20,000. Employer PF at 12% of basic is ₹2,400 and comes out of CTC first, leaving a gross monthly salary of ₹47,600. Employee PF of another ₹2,400 and professional tax of ₹200 are then deducted, so the monthly take-home is ₹45,000, or ₹5,40,000 a year.

Raise basic to 50% on the same CTC and basic becomes ₹25,000. Both PF contributions rise to ₹3,000, gross falls to ₹47,000, and take-home drops to ₹47,000 − ₹3,000 − ₹200 = ₹43,800, which is ₹1,200 less each month. The money is not lost: total [provident fund](/glossary/provident-fund) savings go up from ₹4,800 to ₹6,000 a month.

guide.headline: What changes your real in-hand pay
items: Check the PF line on your payslip. If it is less than 12% of your basic, your employer caps PF at the statutory wage ceiling and your real take-home is higher than shown here.
Take variable pay, joining bonus and employer-paid insurance out of CTC before entering it, because they are not paid to you every month.
Some employers include gratuity in CTC at about 4.81% of basic. It is paid only when you leave after five years, so remove it for a truer monthly figure.
Professional tax is capped at ₹2,500 a year, and some states, such as Delhi, do not levy it at all.
ESI is not deducted here. If your gross pay is within the ESI wage limit, your 0.75% ESI contribution also comes out of each month's pay.
Only the basic percentage moves the result. HRA, special allowance and other allowances are treated as one remainder, so how they are split does not change the figure.

about.headline: Old regime or new regime — know before you choose

It does not account for surcharge on very high incomes, marginal-relief edge cases, or every possible deduction — and tax slabs are typically revised in the Union Budget each year, so always cross-check against the latest official slabs or a chartered accountant/CPA before filing or making a regime decision.

items.question: What are the new tax regime slabs for FY 2025-26?
items.answer: Under the new regime (FY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27): nil up to ₹4,00,000; 5% from ₹4,00,001-8,00,000; 10% from ₹8,00,001-12,00,000; 15% from ₹12,00,001-16,00,000; 20% from ₹16,00,001-20,00,000; 25% from ₹20,00,001-24,00,000; and 30% above ₹24,00,000. items.question: What is the Section 87A rebate?
items.answer: It's a rebate that brings tax liability to zero for taxpayers under a certain taxable income threshold. Under the new regime for FY 2025-26, the rebate generally applies up to ₹12,00,000 taxable income, with marginal relief tapering it just above that threshold. This calculator applies a simplified version and doesn't model every marginal-relief edge case.

items.question: Should I choose the old regime or new regime?
items.answer: It depends on how much you claim in deductions — HRA, 80C investments, home loan interest, and so on. If your eligible deductions are large, the old regime often works out cheaper; if you claim few deductions, the new regime's lower slab rates usually win. Compare both using this calculator with your actual numbers.

items.question: Is this calculator a substitute for filing advice from a CA/CPA?
items.answer: No. This is a simplified estimate for planning purposes only — it excludes surcharge, cess nuances for some cases, and several itemised deductions. For your actual tax filing or a regime decision with real money at stake, verify the latest slabs and consult a qualified chartered accountant/CPA.

items.question: Does the income tax calculator include the standard deduction?
items.answer: Yes. It subtracts ₹75,000 from your gross income for the new regime and ₹50,000 for the old regime before applying the slabs, so enter your income before the standard deduction. That is why a salary of up to ₹12,75,000 shows zero tax under the new regime. Under the law, the standard deduction is available only on salary and pension income.

items.question: Does the calculator include cess and surcharge?
items.answer: It adds 4% health and education cess to the tax under both regimes, so the figures shown already include cess. It does not add surcharge, which applies only when income is above ₹50 lakh. If your income is in that range, your actual tax will be higher than the estimate shown here.

items.question: Is the old regime figure correct for senior citizens?
items.answer: Not exactly. The calculator uses the general old-regime slabs, with no tax on the first ₹2,50,000. Under the old regime, residents aged 60 to 79 have a basic exemption of ₹3,00,000 and those aged 80 or above ₹5,00,000, so the old-regime figure may be higher than they actually owe. New regime slabs are the same at every age, so that figure is unaffected.

items.question: Can I use this calculator for business or freelance income?
items.answer: You can, but enter your taxable profit, not turnover, and expect the result to be low. The calculator always subtracts the ₹75,000 standard deduction, which the law allows only on salary and pension. Near the ₹12 lakh mark the gap is large: ₹12,50,000 of business profit shows nil tax, though about ₹52,000 is due under the new regime. People with business income also face limits on switching regimes, so confirm your choice with a CA/CPA.

cta.subtext: Setu Dine keeps your sales and expense data organised, so tax season is less of a scramble.

guide.headline: Income tax formula used by the calculator
guide.text: **New regime:** Taxable income = Gross income − ₹75,000. Tax = slab tax at 0% up to ₹4 lakh, then 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% on each next ₹4 lakh, and 30% above ₹24 lakh. Tax is nil if taxable income is ₹12,00,000 or less, and above that it is capped at Taxable income − ₹12,00,000. **Old regime:** Taxable income = Gross income − ₹50,000 − Deductions. Tax = slab tax at 0% up to ₹2.5 lakh, 5% up to ₹5 lakh, 20% up to ₹10 lakh and 30% above. Tax is nil if taxable income is ₹5,00,000 or less. In both regimes, Final tax = Tax × 1.04 (4% health and education cess).

guide.headline: How to use the income tax calculator
steps: Enter your annual gross income for the financial year: salary before any deductions, plus other taxable income such as bank interest.
Do not subtract the standard deduction yourself. The calculator takes off ₹75,000 for the new regime and ₹50,000 for the old regime.
In the deductions field, enter the total you can claim under the old regime, such as 80C investments, health insurance, HRA exemption and home loan interest.
Compare the old regime tax and new regime tax figures, both shown including 4% cess.
Read the highlighted figure at the bottom to see which regime saves you money and by how much.

guide.headline: Worked example: ₹15 lakh salary, old vs new regime
paragraphs: Here is how the income tax calculator handles a salaried store manager earning ₹15,00,000 a year who claims ₹2,00,000 of old-regime deductions, such as 80C investments and health insurance. Under the new regime, taxable income is ₹15,00,000 − ₹75,000 = ₹14,25,000. Slab tax is ₹20,000 (5% of ₹4–8 lakh) + ₹40,000 (10% of ₹8–12 lakh) + ₹33,750 (15% of the ₹2,25,000 above ₹12 lakh) = ₹93,750, or ₹97,500 with cess.

Under the old regime, taxable income is ₹15,00,000 − ₹50,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹12,50,000. Slab tax is ₹12,500 (5% of ₹2.5–5 lakh) + ₹1,00,000 (20% of ₹5–10 lakh) + ₹75,000 (30% of the ₹2,50,000 above ₹10 lakh) = ₹1,87,500, or ₹1,95,000 with cess. The new regime saves ₹97,500. At this income, the old regime only comes out cheaper once deductions go above ₹5,43,750, which usually takes HRA exemption and home loan interest on top of full 80C and health insurance claims.

guide.headline: Checks before you choose a regime
items: Enter income before the standard deduction. A salary of up to ₹12,75,000 shows nil tax under the new regime because ₹75,000 comes off first.
Just above the limit, marginal relief caps new-regime tax at the taxable income above ₹12 lakh: a gross salary of ₹12,90,000 shows ₹15,600 with cess, not ₹64,740.
The standard deduction is only for salary and pension. If your income is from business or freelancing, the estimate can be lower than your real tax.
Count only deductions you can back with proof, and remember 80C is capped at ₹1,50,000 a year.
Surcharge, which applies above ₹50 lakh of income, is not included, so treat results at that level as a minimum.
Tell your employer your regime choice at the start of the year so TDS on your salary matches the tax you expect.

about.headline: What gratuity is owed, and when
paragraphs: Gratuity is a lump-sum payment employers owe employees who've completed at least 5 years of continuous service, under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. It's calculated from an employee's last drawn salary and total years of service — not their full career earnings.

This calculator applies the standard formula used for employees covered under the Act, and is useful for both employees estimating what they're owed on exit and owners budgeting for the gratuity liability of long-tenured staff. The statutory ceiling on gratuity is revised periodically by the government, so confirm the current cap before relying on this for a final settlement figure.

items.question: What is the formula for gratuity calculation?
items.answer: Gratuity = (Last Drawn Monthly Salary × 15 × Number of Years of Service) ÷ 26, for employees covered under the Payment of Gratuity Act. Salary here typically means basic pay plus dearness allowance.

items.question: Am I eligible for gratuity?
items.answer: Generally, employees who've completed 5 or more years of continuous service with the same employer are eligible, with some exceptions (such as death or disablement, where the 5-year condition doesn't apply).

items.question: Is there a maximum limit on gratuity?
items.answer: Yes — the Payment of Gratuity Act sets a statutory ceiling on tax-exempt gratuity, which the government revises periodically. Check the current limit before treating this calculator's output as a final, capped figure.

items.question: How is 'years of service' counted if I worked 7 years and 8 months?
items.answer: Under the Act, a period of service of more than 6 months past a completed year is typically rounded up to the next full year. So 7 years 8 months would usually be treated as 8 years for the calculation.

items.question: Which employers have to pay gratuity?
items.answer: The Payment of Gratuity Act covers every factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, port and railway company, and every shop or other establishment that employs 10 or more people, or did on any day in the previous 12 months. Once covered, an employer stays covered even if headcount later falls below 10. Smaller employers can still pay gratuity voluntarily or under an employment contract.

items.question: What salary should I enter in the gratuity calculator?
items.answer: Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, enter the last monthly salary drawn before leaving, counting only basic pay and dearness allowance. Leave out HRA, conveyance, special allowance, bonus, commission and overtime. Your payslip usually shows basic and DA as separate lines, so add just those two. If your company does not pay DA, enter basic pay alone.

items.question: How is gratuity worked out if my employer is not covered by the Act?
items.answer: Employers outside the Act are not bound by its formula. When they do pay gratuity, the tax-exempt part is commonly worked out as half a month's average salary for each completed year, which means a divisor of 30 instead of 26 and no rounding up of part years. This calculator uses the Act's 26-day formula, so it will show a higher figure for that case.

items.question: How soon must an employer pay gratuity after an employee leaves?
items.answer: Under the Act, the employer must work out the gratuity and pay it within 30 days of it becoming payable, which is when employment ends. If payment is late, simple interest is due on the amount for the period of delay. An employee who is not paid can apply to the controlling authority appointed under the Act.

guide.headline: Gratuity formula
guide.text: Gratuity = Last drawn monthly salary (basic + DA) × 15 × Years of service ÷ 26. Gratuity payable = the lower of that figure and ₹20,00,000, the ceiling the calculator applies. When your figure is above the ceiling, the uncapped amount is shown in a note.

guide.headline: How to use the gratuity calculator
steps: Enter the last drawn monthly salary, counting only basic pay plus dearness allowance.
Enter completed years of service as a whole number, adding one year if the final part-year is more than six months.
Read the estimated gratuity payable, which updates as you type.
If the result reaches the ceiling, read the note below it for the uncapped figure.
Change the years to see how much one more year of service adds before an exit date.

guide.headline: Worked example: ₹40,000 basic + DA after 10 years
paragraphs: A restaurant manager leaves with a last drawn [basic salary](/glossary/basic-salary) plus [dearness allowance](/glossary/dearness-allowance) of ₹40,000 a month and 10 years 4 months of service. The extra 4 months is not more than six, so the gratuity calculator is given 10 years. Gratuity = ₹40,000 × 15 × 10 ÷ 26 = ₹60,00,000 ÷ 26 = ₹2,30,769.23. Had the manager stayed to 10 years 8 months, service would count as 11 years and gratuity would be ₹66,00,000 ÷ 26 = ₹2,53,846.15, about ₹23,077 more.

A quick sanity check for any result: 15 ÷ 26 is about 0.577, so each year of service earns a little over half a month's basic + DA. The ceiling only matters at high salaries. A senior employee on ₹2,00,000 a month with 20 years works out to ₹23,07,692.31, so the calculator shows ₹20,00,000 and puts the uncapped figure in a note.

guide.headline: Gratuity tips for employers and employees
items: Keep a gratuity nomination on file for every employee, so the amount can be paid quickly to a nominee if they die in service.
The calculator multiplies whatever you type, so round years of service before entering them rather than typing 7.8.
It does not check the five-year minimum, so confirm the employee is eligible before treating the figure as owed.
Gratuity is worked out on the last drawn salary, so a raise in the final year lifts the whole payout. Budget for that when giving increments to long-serving staff.
Owners with long-serving staff should set aside a yearly provision for gratuity in their books, so a resignation does not become a cash shock.

The labour codes, including the Code on Social Security, 2020, change some gratuity rules, such as eligibility for fixed-term employees and what counts as wages. Ask your CA/CPA which rules apply to your staff.

items.question: How do food delivery platforms calculate commission?
items.answer: Most platforms charge a commission as a percentage of the order value, and may charge GST on top of that commission. Packaging charges and payment gateway fees are typically separate and reduce your payout further.

items.question: Why is my actual payout so much lower than the order value?
items.answer: Commission, GST on commission, packaging cost and payment gateway fees all come out of the order value before you're paid. On a typical order these combined deductions commonly run 25-35% of the order value, depending on your platform and category.

items.question: Should I price items differently for delivery platforms?
items.answer: Many restaurants do build a delivery-specific markup into their aggregator menu prices to offset commission, since dine-in and delivery have very different cost structures. Use this calculator to check whether your current delivery prices leave you a sustainable margin.

items.question: Can Setu Dine manage orders from multiple delivery platforms?

items.question: Can a restaurant claim input tax credit on the GST charged on commission?
items.answer: Most standalone restaurants charge 5% GST on food without input tax credit. That means they cannot set off the GST a platform adds to its commission, so it is a real cost, and the calculator deducts it in full by default. If your business can claim that credit, set GST on commission to 0% to see your payout without the tax you get back. Confirm the treatment with your CA/CPA.

items.question: Does the calculator include discounts and ads I pay for on Swiggy or Zomato?

Packaging is subtracted as a flat rupee amount, so you can add the per-order cost of those charges to the packaging field to get an all-in payout.

items.question: Why does my take-home percentage drop on smaller orders?
items.answer: Commission, GST on commission and the gateway fee are percentages, so they grow and shrink with the order. Packaging is a fixed rupee amount per order. ₹30 of packaging is 10% of a ₹300 order but under 4% of an ₹800 order. Change the order value in the calculator to see how much your take-home moves across your usual order sizes.

items.question: Can I use the commission calculator on my phone?

guide.headline: Online order commission formula
guide.text: Commission = Order value × Commission % ÷ 100. GST on commission = Commission × GST on commission % ÷ 100. Gateway fee = Order value × Gateway fee % ÷ 100. Total deductions = Commission + GST on commission + Gateway fee + Packaging cost. **Real payout = Order value − Total deductions**, and Take-home % = Real payout ÷ Order value × 100. See [aggregator commission](/glossary/aggregator-commission) for what the platform deduction covers.

Enter the platform commission percentage from your aggregator agreement or latest payout report.

guide.headline: Worked example: payout on an ₹800 delivery order
paragraphs: Say a [cloud kitchen](/glossary/cloud-kitchen) gets an ₹800 order on an app charging 22% food delivery commission, with 18% GST on that commission, a 1.8% payment gateway fee and ₹30 of packaging. Commission is ₹800 × 22% = ₹176. GST on commission is ₹176 × 18% = ₹31.68. The gateway fee is ₹800 × 1.8% = ₹14.40. Add the ₹30 packaging and total deductions come to ₹252.08, so the real payout is ₹547.92, a take-home of 68.5%.

Now run a ₹300 order with the same settings. Commission is ₹66, GST on it ₹11.88, the gateway fee ₹5.40 and packaging still ₹30, so deductions total ₹113.28 and the payout is ₹186.72, only 62.2% of the order. Packaging is a fixed rupee cost, so it takes a bigger share of small orders. Work out your smallest common orders separately before you run discounts on them.

guide.headline: Tips for getting a realistic payout figure
items: Take the commission rate from a recent payout report, not the rate card you signed up on. The effective rate on your statement can differ from the headline rate.
If your statement also charges GST on the gateway fee, include it in the gateway field: a 2% fee plus 18% GST is 2.36%.
Work out each platform separately. Commission, gateway fees and packaging rules differ between apps, and a single blended figure can hide a platform that loses you money.
Compare take-home % with your food cost. A 68% take-home on a dish whose food cost is 35% of the order value leaves 33% for rent, staff and profit.
Check the result against one real order from your payout report. If they differ by more than a few rupees, a charge is missing or the commission is charged on a different base.

about.headline: Work backward from your target take-home
paragraphs: If you list the same price online as you charge at the counter, commission, GST on that commission, gateway fees and the GST you owe on the sale all eat into it before you see a rupee — so your online take-home ends up well below your dine-in price.

This calculator flips the usual commission calculation around: enter the amount you actually want to keep per item, plus your platform's charges, and it solves for the listed price that gets you there. Use it whenever you onboard a new item to an aggregator or a platform changes its commission slab.

This is a simplified model — it assumes commission and gateway fees are charged on the listed price and that the listed price is inclusive of the GST you charge on the item. Aggregator agreements vary, so cross-check the result against an actual payout report before rolling out new menu prices.

items.question: Why is the price I should list higher than my dine-in price?
items.answer: Because commission, GST on that commission, gateway fees and the GST you owe on the sale are all deducted from the listed price before you get paid. To net the same amount online as you would at the counter, the listed price has to absorb all of those deductions.

items.question: Is commission really charged on the GST-inclusive price?
items.answer: It depends on the platform and your agreement — some charge commission on the base (pre-GST) value, others on the full listed price. This calculator assumes commission and gateway fees apply to the listed price, which is the more common and conservative case. Check your payout report to confirm which applies to you.

items.question: What if no listed price can cover all the charges?
items.answer: If commission, GST and fees together add up to 100% or more of the listed price, no price can recover your target take-home — the calculator will flag this so you can reconsider the item's online margin instead of guessing at a price.

items.question: Can Setu Dine sync these prices to my delivery platforms?

items.question: What is the difference between the menu price calculator and the commission calculator?

This menu price calculator starts from the amount you want to take home and works back to the price to list. It also takes out the GST included in that price. Use this one to set prices and the other to check payouts.

items.question: How much markup do restaurants need on Swiggy and Zomato prices?
items.answer: There is no single figure, because it depends on your commission, packaging and GST. At this calculator's default inputs (₹200 take-home, 25% commission, 18% GST on commission, 2% gateway fee, ₹20 packaging and 5% GST on food), the listed price comes to ₹345.16, a markup of 72.6%. A lower commission or packaging cost brings that down quickly.

items.question: Can I calculate the listed price for a whole order or combo?
items.answer: Yes. Enter the take-home you want for the whole combo and the packaging cost for all its containers. The formula works the same way for a combo as for a single dish, because commission, gateway fee and GST are all percentages of the listed price, and packaging is a flat amount added to your target.

items.question: What GST rate should I enter for the item?
items.answer: Enter the rate shown on your own tax invoice for that item. The default is 5%, the rate most standalone restaurants charge on food. GST share = Item GST ÷ (1 + Item GST), so 5% GST gives 0.05 ÷ 1.05 = 0.0476 of the listed price. **Markup % = (Listed price − Take-home) ÷ Take-home × 100.** Read more on [tax-inclusive pricing](/glossary/tax-inclusive-pricing).

Enter the payment gateway fee percentage your platform deducts.
Enter the packaging cost for this item in rupees.

guide.headline: Worked example: listing a ₹250 dish on a delivery app
paragraphs: A restaurant sells paneer butter masala for ₹250 plus GST at the counter and wants its Zomato and Swiggy menu price to leave the same ₹250 on every order. Its platform charges 22% commission plus 18% GST on it and a 2% gateway fee, and the container costs ₹25. With 5% GST on food, the GST share of the listed price is 0.05 ÷ 1.05 = 0.04762. Commission with its GST is 0.22 × 1.18 = 0.2596. The bracket is 1 − 0.04762 − 0.2596 − 0.02 = 0.67278, so the listed price is (₹250 + ₹25) ÷ 0.67278 = ₹408.75, a 63.5% markup.

Check it the other way. The ₹408.75 listing carries ₹19.46 of GST, ₹106.11 of commission plus GST, and ₹33.18 of gateway fee plus packaging. That is ₹158.75 of deductions, which leaves exactly ₹250. This kind of [menu price padding](/glossary/menu-price-padding) only works if you round up: list it at ₹409 or a little more, never less, because rounding down misses the target on every order.

guide.headline: Before you upload new prices
items: Round the listed price up to the next clean figure. Rounding down puts every order below your take-home target.
Packaging is added to your target before the deductions are grossed up, so it costs more than its face value. In the example above, the ₹25 container adds about ₹37 to the listed price.
Price combos and single items separately. Commission is a percentage but packaging is per container, so a combo packed in one box needs less markup than the same dishes sold one by one.
If your statement charges GST on the gateway fee, include it in the gateway field: a 2% fee plus 18% GST is 2.36%.
Keep a note of the target take-home behind each listed price, so you can rerun an item quickly when commission or GST rates change.

about.headline: Cost the recipe, not just the headline ingredients
paragraphs: Most menu pricing mistakes come from costing a dish on its 2-3 main ingredients and guessing the rest. Oil, spices, garnish and packaging are individually small but add up — and that gap compounds across hundreds of orders a month.

Add every ingredient in a recipe with what the amount you use costs you to get an accurate total cost and cost per serving. Once you know the real cost, use it alongside the food cost percentage calculator to set a menu price that protects your margin.

items.question: Why should I cost every ingredient instead of just the main ones?
items.answer: Small ingredients like oil, spices, sauces and garnish are individually cheap but add up across a recipe, and across hundreds of plates sold each month that gap can meaningfully erode margin if it's never accounted for.

items.question: How many servings should I divide the total cost by?
items.answer: Divide by the actual number of servings or plates the recipe yields, not the number of ingredients used. If a batch recipe makes a base used across 10 plates, use 10 as the serving count.

items.question: Does this include labour or overhead cost?
items.answer: No — this calculates raw ingredient cost only. Add labour and overhead separately, and consider both alongside ingredient cost when setting a final menu price.

items.question: Can I save this for every dish on my menu?
items.answer: This tool doesn't store data between sessions, so note down the cost per serving for each dish as you go. Setu Dine can store recipe costs against menu items permanently and update automatically as ingredient prices change.

items.question: How do I account for peeling, trimming or cooking loss in recipe cost?
items.answer: Base the cost on the usable weight, not the weight you bought. If 1 kg of onions costing ₹40 gives 900 g after peeling, each usable kilo costs ₹40 ÷ 0.9 = ₹44.44, so 200 g of peeled onion in the recipe costs about ₹8.89. Enter that figure in Cost used. Apply the same logic to chicken on the bone, fish and leafy greens, where the loss is usually larger.

items.question: What target food cost percentage should I enter?
items.answer: Enter the share of the menu price you can afford to spend on ingredients once labour, rent and other running costs are covered. The calculator starts at 30%, and many restaurants work somewhere in the 25% to 35% range depending on format. A lower target gives a higher suggested price: a ₹50 plate cost needs a ₹200 price at 25%, but only ₹166.67 at 30%.

items.question: Can I cost a base gravy or batter that goes into several dishes?
items.answer: Yes. Cost the base as its own recipe first: enter its ingredients and set Servings to the number of portions the batch gives, for example 20 ladles of makhani gravy. The cost per serving is then your cost per ladle. In each dish that uses the gravy, add one row with that per-ladle cost instead of listing the gravy ingredients again.

items.question: Is the recipe costing calculator free, and does it work on a phone?
items.answer: Yes. It is free to use with no signup or download, and it runs in any modern mobile or desktop browser. The ingredient rows, servings and target fields fit a phone screen and the results recalculate as you type, so you can cost a dish standing in the kitchen or at the market. All the calculation happens in your browser.

cta.headline: Recipes that update cost automatically
cta.subtext: Setu Dine links recipes to live ingredient prices, so cost per plate stays accurate without manual recalculation.

guide.headline: Recipe cost formula
guide.text: Total recipe cost = sum of the Cost used in every ingredient row. Cost per serving = Total recipe cost ÷ Servings this recipe yields. Suggested price per serving = Cost per serving ÷ (Target food cost % ÷ 100). The cost per serving is your [plate cost](/glossary/plate-cost), the figure every menu price should start from.

guide.headline: How to use the recipe costing calculator
steps: Replace the sample rows (Paneer, Spices & sauces, Oil & garnish) with your own ingredients, typing each name in the Ingredient column.
In Cost used, enter the rupee cost of the quantity that goes into this recipe, not the price of the whole pack. For example, 250 g of paneer from a ₹400 per kg block is ₹100.
Tap Add ingredient for every extra item, including oil, spices, garnish and packaging. Use the cross next to a row to remove it.
Enter Servings this recipe yields, the number of plates the batch actually produces.
Set Target food cost % to the share of the menu price you want ingredients to take. It starts at 30%.
Read Total recipe cost (all servings), Cost per serving and Suggested price per serving. They update as you type.

guide.headline: Worked example: costing a 10-plate batch of paneer butter masala
paragraphs: Say your kitchen makes paneer butter masala in batches of 10 plates. In the recipe costing calculator, enter five rows: paneer ₹400 (1 kg, so 100 g a plate), tomato, onion and cashew gravy ₹110, butter and cream ₹120, spices and kasuri methi ₹30, and oil and garnish ₹20. Total recipe cost is ₹680, and with Servings set to 10 the cost per serving is ₹680 ÷ 10 = ₹68. Paneer alone is ₹40 of that, more than half the plate cost, so a paneer price rise is the first thing to watch.

At the default 30% target, the suggested price per serving is ₹68 ÷ 0.30 = ₹226.67. A menu price of ₹229 keeps food cost just under target (₹68 ÷ ₹229 = 29.7%). If a 35% food cost suits your format, the suggested price drops to ₹68 ÷ 0.35 = ₹194.29. Once you settle on a price, check its food cost % and gross profit in the [food cost percentage calculator](/calculators/food-cost-calculator).

guide.headline: Recipe costing mistakes to avoid
items: Using an old purchase price. Vegetable, dairy and oil prices move week to week, so recost a dish whenever your supplier bill changes.
Dividing by planned portions. Count the plates the batch actually gives after cooking and plating, not the number written on the recipe card.
Skipping packaging on delivery dishes. Add the container, lid, bag and cutlery as their own rows when you cost the takeaway version.
Costing a 100 g portion while the line plates 120 g. Weigh a few portions during service and correct the recipe quantities if they drift.

Reading the suggested price as GST-inclusive. The calculator adds no GST, so treat it as your price before tax: add GST on top for a tax-exclusive menu, or check that a GST-inclusive menu price still leaves this amount after tax.
Leaving out transport and loading charges. If you pay to bring stock in, spread that cost into the ingredient prices you enter.
