about.headline: The bar's version of food cost percentage
paragraphs: Pour cost is to a bar what food cost percentage is to a kitchen — the share of a drink's selling price that goes toward the liquor itself. It's the number that tells you whether your drink pricing and pour sizes are actually profitable, especially once you factor in how many pours a single bottle yields.

Enter the bottle cost, bottle size, the pour size you actually serve, and the selling price per drink to get pour cost %, profit per pour and how many pours you should get from each bottle. Run your top sellers through this whenever a supplier changes a price.

items.question: How is pour cost percentage calculated?
items.answer: Pour Cost % = (Cost per Pour ÷ Selling Price per Pour) × 100, where Cost per Pour = Bottle Cost ÷ (Bottle Size ÷ Pour Size).

items.question: What is a good pour cost percentage?
items.answer: Most bars target 18-24% pour cost on spirits, though it varies by category — premium and craft offerings often run a bit higher in exchange for a higher price point and perceived value.

items.question: Why does my actual pour cost not match my target?
items.answer: Over-pouring is the most common cause — even an extra 5-10ml per drink compounds quickly across a busy night. Inconsistent pour sizes, spillage, and complimentary or comped drinks also widen the gap between target and actual pour cost.

items.question: How many pours should I get from one bottle?
items.answer: Pours per Bottle = Bottle Size ÷ Pour Size. A standard 750ml bottle poured at 30ml per drink should yield 25 pours — track actual pours against this to spot over-pouring or wastage.

items.question: How do I calculate the cost of a 60 ml large peg?
items.answer: Enter 60 as the Pour size and the large-peg menu price as the Selling price per pour. A 750 ml bottle gives 12.5 large pegs. The Pours per bottle result is rounded to a whole number on screen, so it shows 13, but cost per pour uses the exact 12.5, so a ₹1,800 bottle works out to ₹144 per large peg.

items.question: Does pour cost include mixers, soda, ice or garnish?
items.answer: No. The calculator covers only the liquor in the pour, based on bottle cost and bottle size. For a cocktail or a whisky-soda, work out the spirit cost here, then add the cost of mixers, syrups, fruit and garnish separately, for example with the recipe costing calculator, and compare the full drink cost against its menu price.

items.question: Can I use the pour cost calculator for wine by the glass or beer?
items.answer: Yes. For wine, enter the bottle size (usually 750 ml) and your glass measure, such as 150 ml, which gives 5 glasses per bottle. For bottled beer sold whole, enter the same number in Bottle size and Pour size, so pours per bottle is 1 and cost per pour equals the bottle cost. For draught beer, enter the keg size in ml and your glass size.

items.question: What is the difference between pour cost percentage and profit per pour?
items.answer: Pour cost % is the share of the selling price spent on liquor; profit per pour is the rupee amount left over. They can point in different directions. A ₹250 peg costing ₹50 runs at 20% and leaves ₹200, while a ₹900 single malt peg costing ₹270 runs at 30% yet leaves ₹630. Look at both before deciding which drinks to push.

guide.headline: Pour cost formula
guide.text: Pours per bottle = Bottle size (ml) ÷ Pour size (ml). Cost per pour = Bottle cost ÷ Pours per bottle. Pour cost % = Cost per pour ÷ Selling price per pour × 100. Profit per pour = Selling price per pour − Cost per pour, which is what is left after the liquor alone, before mixers, staff or rent.

guide.headline: How to use the liquor pour cost calculator
steps: Enter Bottle cost, the price you pay for one bottle including delivery and any taxes on your purchase bill.
Enter Bottle size in ml, such as 750 for a full bottle, 375 for a half or 180 for a quarter.
Enter Pour size in ml, the measure you serve, such as 30 ml for a small peg or 60 ml for a large peg.
Enter Selling price per pour, the menu price for that measure.
Read Pour cost %, Profit per pour, Cost per pour and Pours per bottle. Pours per bottle is rounded to a whole number on screen, but the other results use the exact figure.

guide.headline: Worked example: a ₹1,800 whisky bottle sold in 30 ml pegs
paragraphs: A bar pays ₹1,800 for a 750 ml bottle of whisky and sells it at ₹300 per 30 ml peg. The liquor cost calculator shows 750 ÷ 30 = 25 pours per bottle, a cost per pour of ₹1,800 ÷ 25 = ₹72, a [pour cost](/glossary/pour-cost) of ₹72 ÷ ₹300 × 100 = 24%, and a profit per pour of ₹300 − ₹72 = ₹228. Selling all 25 pegs brings in ₹7,500 from the bottle.

Now suppose pegs are free-poured at about 35 ml. Change Pour size to 35 and the bottle gives only 21.4 pours (shown as 21), cost per pour rises to ₹84, pour cost climbs to 28% and profit per peg falls to ₹216. Each peg still sells for ₹300, so the bottle now earns about ₹6,429 instead of ₹7,500, roughly ₹1,071 lost per bottle. That is why [portion control](/glossary/portion-control) with a proper peg measure matters as much as the menu price.

guide.headline: Bar cost control checklist
items: Pour with a peg measure or jigger for every drink. Free pouring is where most extra millilitres go.
Enter the bottle price from your latest purchase bill, and update it when supplier or state excise prices change.
Measure or weigh open bottles at each stock count, and compare the pours your billing recorded with the pours each bottle should have given.
Record comps, spillage and breakage separately so they do not hide inside an over-pouring problem.
Recheck pour cost before a happy hour. A ₹300 peg costing ₹72 runs at 24%, but at a ₹200 happy-hour price the same peg runs at 36%.

hero.headline: Tip Split Calculator
hero.subheadline: Add your staff and split a shared tip pool equally, by hours worked, or by points/shares.

about.headline: Tip pooling that staff can see is fair
paragraphs: Splitting tips manually gets messy fast once you're accounting for different shift lengths or roles. A server who worked a full double shift and one who covered the last two hours shouldn't get equal shares — but agreeing on exactly how to weight it is where most disputes start.

This calculator splits a tip pool three ways: equally across everyone, proportionally by hours worked, or by a points/shares system where you assign each role or person a weight. Add your staff, pick a method, and the split updates instantly.

items.question: What's the difference between an equal split and a points-based split?
items.answer: An equal split divides the pool evenly regardless of role or hours. A points-based split assigns each person a weight (points or shares) reflecting role, seniority or hours, and divides the pool proportionally to those weights — common when front-of-house and support roles are pooled together.

items.question: Should kitchen staff be included in a tip pool with servers?
items.answer: Tip pooling rules and norms vary by region and by local labour regulations — some jurisdictions restrict who can be included in a tip pool. Check what's permitted where you operate before deciding who's eligible.

items.question: How do I split tips fairly by hours worked?
items.answer: Use the 'by hours' method — enter each person's hours for the shift or period, and the pool is divided proportionally, so someone who worked twice as long receives roughly twice the share.

items.question: Can I use this for a single shift or a whole week's tips?
items.answer: Either — enter the total tip pool for whatever period you're splitting (a shift, a day, a week) along with the hours or shares for that same period.

items.question: How do I split tips between front-of-house and kitchen staff?
items.answer: Run the calculator twice. First choose By hours / shares and add two rows, Floor and Kitchen, with the agreed shares, such as 7 and 3, so a ₹10,000 pool splits into ₹7,000 and ₹3,000. Then run each group's amount across its own staff by hours or points. Agree the group shares with the team before the period starts.

items.question: Can I split tips by fixed percentages?
items.answer: Yes. Choose By hours / shares and enter each person's percentage in the Hours / shares column, for example 50, 30 and 20. Because each entry is divided by the total of all entries, a ₹6,000 pool pays ₹3,000, ₹1,800 and ₹1,200. If your percentages do not add up to 100, the calculator scales them proportionally, so the full pool is still paid out.

items.question: Is the tip split calculator free to use on a phone?
items.answer: Yes. It is free, needs no signup or app, and runs in your phone's browser, so you can settle tips at the counter at the end of a shift. The calculator does not save staff names or amounts between visits, so re-enter them each time or keep a screenshot of the payout list as your record.

items.question: Can I use this to split a service charge collected on bills?
items.answer: The calculator splits whatever amount you enter, so it works the same way for a service charge pool as for tips. Whether you can charge it is a separate matter: in India, consumer protection guidelines say a service charge cannot be added to a bill automatically or made compulsory for the guest. Check the current rules before you bill it.

guide.headline: Tip split formula
guide.text: Equal split: each person's share = Total tip pool ÷ number of staff rows. By hours / shares: each person's share = Total tip pool × (that person's hours or shares ÷ total hours or shares of everyone listed). In both modes the payouts add up to the full pool, as long as at least one person has hours or shares entered in the weighted mode. See [tip pooling](/glossary/tip-pooling) for the common ways pools are set up.

Enter the Total tip pool, including any card or UPI tips you are pooling with cash.

If you chose By hours / shares, enter each person's hours worked or agreed points in the Hours / shares column. Equal split ignores this column.
Read each person's payout in the list below. Amounts show to the paisa and change as you type.

guide.headline: Worked example: splitting a ₹12,000 weekly tip pool
paragraphs: A café collects ₹12,000 in tips over a week, cash and UPI together. Four people shared the floor, and the [shift roster](/glossary/shift-roster) shows Riya worked 40 hours, Arjun 30, Meena 30 and Sameer 20, a total of 120 hours. Choose By hours / shares, enter the pool and the hours, and the tip split calculator works out ₹100 per hour: Riya ₹4,000, Arjun ₹3,000, Meena ₹3,000 and Sameer ₹2,000. An equal split would pay everyone ₹3,000, moving ₹1,000 from Riya to Sameer.

If the team agrees on role points instead, enter those in the same column. With Riya as captain on 3 shares, Arjun and Meena on 2 each and Sameer as helper on 1, there are 8 shares worth ₹1,500 each, so the payouts are ₹4,500, ₹3,000, ₹3,000 and ₹1,500. To weight by both role and hours, multiply them before entering: 40 hours × 3 points = 120 for Riya.

guide.headline: Tip pooling checklist for managers
items: Agree the method (equal, by hours or by points) with staff before the period starts, and write it down.
Take hours from your attendance register or shift roster for the same dates as the pool, not from memory.
Remove the row of anyone who was not on shift, and any blank row. In Equal split every row gets a share, even one with 0 hours or no name.
Shares show to the paisa, so round payouts to convenient amounts and carry the small remainder into the next pool.
Show the team the payout list, even a screenshot, so everyone can see how the split was worked out.

hero.headline: Inventory Turnover Calculator
hero.subheadline: Enter cost of goods sold and average inventory value to see your turnover ratio and days of stock on hand.

about.headline: Cash tied up on a shelf is cash you can't use elsewhere
paragraphs: Inventory turnover tells you how many times you sell through your average stock in a given period. A low turnover ratio usually means cash sitting in slow-moving stock; a very high one can mean you're at risk of stockouts. Neither extreme is automatically good — the right number depends on your category and how easily you can restock.

Enter your cost of goods sold for a period (month or year) and your average inventory value over the same period to get your turnover ratio and the equivalent number of days of stock you're holding. Track this over time rather than in isolation — a falling turnover ratio is often the earliest sign of slow-moving or dead stock building up.

items.question: What is the inventory turnover ratio formula?
items.answer: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory Value, for the same period. Average inventory is typically (Opening Inventory + Closing Inventory) ÷ 2.

items.question: What is a good inventory turnover ratio?
items.answer: It varies widely by category — perishables and fast fashion turn over much faster than furniture or electronics. Compare your ratio against your own historical trend and category benchmarks rather than a single universal number.

items.question: What does 'days inventory outstanding' mean?
items.answer: It's the turnover ratio converted into days — roughly how many days of sales your current average inventory represents. It's calculated as 365 ÷ Inventory Turnover Ratio, and a rising number signals stock is moving more slowly than before.

items.question: Why is my inventory turnover dropping?
items.answer: Common causes are overstocking ahead of demand, slow-moving SKUs accumulating, seasonal demand dips, or pricing that's no longer competitive enough to move stock at the previous pace.

items.question: Should I use sales or cost of goods sold to calculate inventory turnover?
items.answer: Use cost of goods sold. Inventory is valued at cost, so dividing sales by it mixes two bases and inflates the ratio by your margin. A store with ₹1,50,000 average stock, ₹4,50,000 cost of goods sold and ₹6,30,000 sales shows 3x on cost but 4.2x on sales. If you have to use sales because COGS is not available, use sales in every period so the results still compare.

items.question: How do I calculate monthly inventory turnover?
items.answer: Enter the month's cost of goods sold, the average stock value for that month, and 30 (or the actual number of days) in the days in period field. The ratio is per month, so if sales and stock levels stay similar all year, a monthly turnover of 1x works out to about 12x a year. Days inventory outstanding is always in days, so you can compare it across periods of different lengths.

items.question: How do I calculate cost of goods sold for a shop?
items.answer: For a trading business, cost of goods sold is opening stock, plus purchases during the period, plus direct costs such as freight inward, minus closing stock. Value everything at cost, excluding GST you claim as input tax credit. You can usually get these figures from your accountant's trading account or the stock reports in your accounting software.

items.question: How can I improve my inventory turnover ratio?
items.answer: Order slow-moving items in smaller quantities more often, stop reordering items that have not sold in months, and clear dead stock with markdowns or bundles. Rank items by the stock value you hold so you deal first with the ones that tie up the most cash. Recalculate each month to see whether the changes are working.

guide.headline: Inventory turnover and days of stock formula
guide.text: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of goods sold ÷ Average inventory value. Days inventory outstanding = Days in period ÷ Inventory turnover ratio. Take both money figures from the same period, valued at cost, and set **Days in period** to match: 30 for a month, 90 for a quarter, 365 for a year. See [COGS](/glossary/cogs) and [inventory turnover](/glossary/inventory-turnover) for the terms.

guide.headline: How to use the Inventory Turnover Calculator
steps: Decide the period you want to measure, such as a month, a quarter or a financial year, and pull your figures for that period only.
Enter cost of goods sold for the period, valued at purchase cost rather than selling price.
Enter the average inventory value at cost for the same period.
Enter the days in the period, for example 30, 90 or 365.
Read the inventory turnover ratio, shown as times (such as 3x), and days inventory outstanding.
Note the result, then repeat for earlier periods or separate categories and compare the numbers.

guide.headline: Worked example: inventory turnover for a general store's quarter
paragraphs: A general store's books for a 90-day quarter show cost of goods sold of ₹4,50,000. Stock at cost was ₹1,40,000 at the start of the quarter and ₹1,60,000 at the end, so average inventory is (₹1,40,000 + ₹1,60,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,50,000. Inventory turnover for the quarter is ₹4,50,000 ÷ ₹1,50,000 = 3x. With 90 days in the period, days inventory outstanding is 90 ÷ 3 = 30 days, so the store holds about a month of stock.

If the owner entered sales of ₹6,30,000 instead of cost of goods sold, the calculator would show 4.2x and 21 days. Sales include your margin while inventory is valued at cost, so using sales makes stock look faster-moving than it really is. Keep both figures at cost to get a number you can compare from one quarter to the next.

guide.headline: Common mistakes that distort turnover
items: Mixing bases: cost of goods sold at cost but inventory at MRP or selling price, or the other way round.
Entering 365 days when the cost of goods sold covers only a month or a quarter.
Using cost of goods sold for all outlets and the godown but stock from only one of them. Both figures must cover the same locations.
Including GST you claim as input tax credit in stock or purchase values. GST you get back is not part of inventory cost.
Averaging only opening and closing stock for a seasonal business. Average the month-end stock values across the period instead.
Running only one store-wide figure. A healthy overall ratio can hide dead stock sitting in one category.

about.headline: Reorder before you run out, not after
paragraphs: A reorder point is the stock level that should trigger a new purchase order — set it too low and you risk running out before the new stock arrives; set it too high and you're tying up cash in excess inventory.

Enter your average daily sales for an item, how many days your supplier typically takes to deliver, and a safety stock buffer for demand spikes or delivery delays, and this calculator gives you the exact unit count that should trigger your next order.

items.question: What is the reorder point formula?
items.answer: Reorder Point = (Average Daily Sales × Supplier Lead Time in Days) + Safety Stock. It's the stock level at which a new order should be placed so the replacement stock arrives before you run out.

items.question: How do I decide on a safety stock number?
items.answer: Safety stock should cover both demand variability (busier-than-average days) and supplier delays. A common starting approach is a few days' worth of average sales, adjusted up for items with unreliable suppliers or volatile demand.

items.question: What if my supplier's lead time varies a lot?
items.answer: Use your worst realistic lead time rather than the best case when calculating the reorder point, and lean on a larger safety stock buffer for items where lead time is unpredictable.

items.question: Does this account for seasonal demand spikes?
items.answer: Not directly — this uses your average daily sales figure. For seasonal items, recalculate using the average daily sales expected during the upcoming season rather than a flat annual average.

items.question: What is the difference between reorder point and safety stock?
items.answer: Safety stock is the buffer you want left on the shelf when a new delivery arrives, to cover busy days or a late supplier. The reorder point is the stock level at which you place an order. It includes that buffer plus the stock you expect to sell while you wait for delivery. In this calculator, reorder point equals lead-time demand plus safety stock.

items.question: How do I calculate average daily sales for one item?
items.answer: Add up the units of that item sold over a recent period, such as the last 30 days, and divide by the number of days. If your shop closes one day a week, either divide by the days you were open and count lead time in working days too, or use calendar days for both. Mixing the two makes the reorder point too high or too low.

items.question: Can I use the reorder point calculator for restaurant ingredients?
items.answer: Yes. Enter average daily usage instead of sales, such as kilograms of onions or litres of milk used per day, along with the supplier's lead time and a safety buffer. The fields are labelled in units, but any unit works as long as daily usage and safety stock use the same one.

items.question: What happens if I set safety stock to zero?
items.answer: The reorder point then equals lead-time demand, so on an average day the last unit sells just as the delivery arrives. A busier day or a late delivery means you run out. Zero safety stock can work for items you can buy locally the same day, or ones customers will not miss. For fast sellers, keep at least a day or two of sales as a buffer.

guide.headline: Reorder point and lead-time demand formula
guide.text: Lead-time demand = Average daily sales × Supplier lead time in days. **Reorder point = Lead-time demand + Safety stock.** Both results are shown rounded to whole units. When stock on hand falls to the [reorder point](/glossary/reorder-point), place the next order. See [lead time](/glossary/lead-time) and [safety stock](/glossary/safety-stock) for the other terms.

guide.headline: How to use the Stock Reorder Point Calculator
steps: Pick one item. Reorder points are set per item (SKU), not for the whole shop.
Enter average daily sales in units: units sold over the last few weeks divided by the number of days.
Enter supplier lead time in days, from the day you place the order to the day the stock is ready to sell.
Enter safety stock in units, the buffer you want left when the new stock arrives.
Read Reorder at for the trigger level, and Lead-time demand for how much you expect to sell while you wait.
Write the reorder point in your stock register or on the shelf tag, and order as soon as stock falls to it.

guide.headline: Worked example: reorder point for cooking oil pouches
paragraphs: A kirana store sells about 18 one-litre sunflower oil pouches a day, and its distributor takes 4 days to deliver. Lead-time demand is 18 × 4 = 72 pouches. The owner keeps two days of sales as safety stock, 18 × 2 = 36 pouches, so the reorder point is 72 + 36 = 108. When the count drops to 108 pouches, it is time to call the distributor.

Before Diwali, sales rise to 25 pouches a day and deliveries take 6 days. Lead-time demand becomes 25 × 6 = 150, and two days of safety stock is now 50, so the reorder point jumps to 200. If the owner kept the old figure of 108 that season, the shelf would run empty nearly two days before the new stock arrived.

guide.headline: Tips for reorder points that hold up
items: Base average daily sales on the last four to eight weeks, and leave out one-off bulk orders that will not repeat.
Count only sellable stock against the reorder point. Exclude damaged, expired or already-reserved units.
Work in the unit you order in. If the supplier sells by the carton, convert the reorder point from pieces to cartons.
If you count stock only once a week, add up to a week of sales to the reorder point so an item cannot slip below it unnoticed between counts.
Review reorder points every month, and straight away when you switch supplier or delivery days change.
The reorder point tells you when to order, not how much. How much to order depends on the supplier's minimum order, your shelf space and the cash you have.

about.headline: The number that tells you if marketing is working
paragraphs: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) is the average amount you spend to win one new customer, across all the marketing and sales costs that went into acquiring them. It only means something next to a second number — what that customer is actually worth to you.

Enter your total spend over a period and the number of new customers it brought in to get your CAC. If you also know the average revenue per customer, this calculator shows the ratio between the two — a quick gut-check on whether a campaign or channel is actually paying for itself.

items.question: What is the CAC formula?
items.answer: CAC = Total Marketing and Sales Spend ÷ Number of New Customers Acquired, over the same period. Spending ₹50,000 to acquire 100 new customers gives a CAC of ₹500.

items.question: What costs should I include in marketing spend?
items.answer: Include ad spend, agency or platform fees, promotional discounts used purely for acquisition, and a reasonable share of sales team cost if relevant — anything spent specifically to bring in new customers during that period.

items.question: What's a good CAC?
items.answer: It depends entirely on what a customer is worth to you over time. A CAC is healthy if it's comfortably below the revenue (ideally repeat revenue) a typical customer generates — there's no fixed 'good' number across businesses.

items.question: How is CAC different from average order value?
items.answer: CAC measures what you spent to win a customer; average order value measures what a customer spends per order once acquired. Comparing the two tells you roughly how many orders it takes to recover your acquisition cost.

items.question: What does the revenue-to-CAC ratio mean?
items.answer: It shows how many rupees of revenue a typical new customer brings in for every rupee spent acquiring them. The calculator divides your average revenue per customer by the CAC. A ratio of 4x means ₹4 of revenue for each ₹1 of acquisition cost, while anything below 1x means customers bring in less than they cost to win. Because it uses revenue, multiply by your gross margin before judging profitability.

items.question: What is the difference between CAC and ROAS?
items.answer: ROAS, or return on ad spend, divides the revenue a campaign generated by what you spent on the ads, counting every sale it drove, including repeat buyers. CAC divides total acquisition spend by the number of new customers won. ROAS tells you whether a campaign paid back in sales; CAC tells you the price of each new customer, which you then compare with what that customer is worth over time.

items.question: How do I calculate CAC if I don't spend on ads?
items.answer: Add up whatever you spent to attract first-time customers: referral rewards, free samples, printed flyers, a stall at a local event or a housing society notice-board campaign. Divide that by the new customers who came in during the same period. Word-of-mouth customers cost little to win, but tracking CAC still tells you whether a referral reward or sampling drive is worth continuing.

items.question: How is customer lifetime value related to CAC?
items.answer: Customer lifetime value is the total profit a customer is expected to bring in over the whole time they buy from you, while CAC is the one-time cost of winning them. Comparing the two shows whether acquisition pays off in the long run. An LTV-to-CAC ratio of around 3:1 is a commonly quoted target, though what works for you depends on your margins and cash flow.

guide.headline: Customer acquisition cost formula
guide.text: CAC = Marketing & sales spend ÷ New customers acquired, for the same period. Revenue-to-CAC ratio = Average revenue per customer ÷ CAC. The ratio is shown only when you enter an average revenue figure; leave that field empty and it shows a dash.

guide.headline: How to use the CAC calculator
steps: Choose one period, such as a month, a quarter or the length of a single campaign, and use it for every figure.
Enter Marketing & sales spend: the total you spent in that period to win new customers.
Enter New customers acquired: first-time customers only, not repeat visits or returning patients.
Optionally enter Average revenue per customer, ideally what a new customer spends with you over a fixed window such as their first six months.
Read Customer acquisition cost and the Revenue-to-CAC ratio. A ratio below 1x means a typical customer brings in less revenue than it cost to win them.
Repeat with the spend and new-customer count for each channel to see which one is cheapest.

guide.headline: Worked example: CAC for a clinic spending ₹30,000 a month
paragraphs: A physiotherapy clinic spends ₹20,000 on Google ads and ₹10,000 on a local newspaper insert in one month, and gets 80 new patients. Entered as one total, the CAC calculator gives ₹30,000 ÷ 80 = ₹375 per new patient. If a new patient spends ₹1,500 on average over a course of treatment, the revenue-to-CAC ratio is ₹1,500 ÷ ₹375 = 4x.

Run the channels separately and the picture changes. The ads brought 64 patients, a CAC of ₹312.50 and a ratio of 4.8x. The newspaper brought 16, a CAC of ₹625 and a ratio of 2.4x. The ratio uses revenue, not profit. If the clinic keeps 40% of revenue after consumables and therapist pay, the newspaper returns ₹0.96 of gross profit for every ₹1 spent (2.4 × 40%), so it does not quite pay for itself, while the ads return ₹1.92. Comparing CAC with [customer lifetime value](/glossary/customer-lifetime-value) rather than one course of treatment makes this kind of call clearer.

guide.headline: Tips for an accurate CAC
items: Count only first-time customers. Including repeat visits inflates the customer count and makes CAC look lower than it is.
Allow for delay. Customers often arrive weeks after you pay for ads, so measure over a full month or quarter rather than a few days.
Tag every new customer's source, by asking at billing or giving each channel its own coupon code, so you can calculate CAC per channel.
Compare against gross profit, not just revenue. Multiply the revenue-to-CAC ratio by your gross margin to see how much gross profit each rupee of marketing returns.
Do not judge a channel on first-bill revenue alone. A low ratio on the first visit can still work if those customers return regularly, so check their repeat rate before cutting it.
Track CAC every month. A steady rise on the same channel can mean the audience has tired of the ad or offer, or that more competitors are targeting the same customers.

about.headline: A small AOV increase compounds fast
paragraphs: Average order value (AOV) is the average amount spent per order — and it's one of the few revenue levers you can move without acquiring a single new customer. A combo offer, a well-placed add-on suggestion, or a small price adjustment can lift AOV across every order you already get.

Enter your total revenue and number of orders for a period to find your current AOV, then enter a target percentage increase to see what that lift would be worth in extra revenue at the same order volume — useful for justifying whether an upsell push or menu/bundle change is worth the effort.

items.question: What is the average order value formula?
items.answer: AOV = Total Revenue ÷ Number of Orders, for the same period. ₹5,00,000 in revenue across 1,000 orders gives an AOV of ₹500.

items.question: How can I increase average order value?
items.answer: Common levers include combo or bundle offers, upselling a larger size or add-on at the point of order, minimum-spend free delivery thresholds, and prominently suggesting complementary items alongside what a customer is already ordering.

items.question: Why does a small AOV increase matter so much?
items.answer: Because it applies to every order you already get, with no additional acquisition cost — a 10% AOV lift on your existing order volume drops straight to extra revenue, without needing a single new customer.

items.question: Is a higher AOV always better?
items.answer: Generally yes for revenue, but check it doesn't come at the cost of order frequency or customer satisfaction — pushing add-ons too aggressively can backfire. Track AOV alongside repeat order rate to catch that early.

items.question: What is the difference between AOV and average spend per cover?
items.answer: AOV is revenue per order or bill, while average spend per cover is revenue per guest. For dine-in they can tell different stories: a ₹1,200 bill from a table of four is ₹300 a head, but the same bill from two guests is ₹600 a head. Restaurants usually track both, using AOV for takeaway and delivery and spend per cover for the dining room.

items.question: Is average order value the same as basket size?
items.answer: No. Basket size is the average number of items per bill, while average order value is the average amount spent per bill. They usually move together, but not always: a customer who swaps two cheap items for one premium dish lowers basket size and raises AOV. Watching both shows whether an upsell push is adding items or simply moving customers to pricier ones.

items.question: Where do I find total revenue and number of orders for the AOV calculator?
items.answer: Your POS or billing software's sales report for the period shows both: total sales and the count of bills or invoices. Exclude cancelled and voided bills. For delivery apps, take the delivered orders and their food value before GST from the partner dashboard, not your payout after commission, and run those orders separately from dine-in so the two AOVs stay comparable.

items.question: What is a good average order value for a restaurant or shop?
items.answer: There is no single good figure. A tea stall, a quick-service outlet and a fine-dining restaurant will have AOVs that differ many times over, and a kirana store differs from a clothing shop in the same way. The useful comparison is your own AOV over time and by channel. Track it monthly and judge the effect of each menu, pricing or combo change against that history.

guide.headline: Average order value formula
guide.text: AOV = Total revenue ÷ Number of orders, for the same period. AOV at target increase = AOV × (1 + Target AOV increase % ÷ 100). Extra revenue = (AOV at target − AOV) × Number of orders, assuming order volume stays the same.

steps: Pick a period, such as a day, a week or a month, and pull its sales figure from your billing or POS report.
Enter Total revenue (period). Use sales before GST and leave out cancelled or refunded orders.
Enter Number of orders: the count of completed bills or invoices in the same period.
Enter Target AOV increase as a percentage, for example 8 for an 8% lift.
Read Current AOV, AOV at target increase and Extra revenue, same order volume.
Change the target percentage to see what a smaller or larger lift would be worth before you settle on an upsell plan.

guide.headline: Worked example: AOV for a restaurant with 1,600 monthly orders
paragraphs: A restaurant takes ₹6,40,000 over 1,600 orders in a month. The AOV calculator shows a current average order value of ₹400 (₹6,40,000 ÷ 1,600). With a target AOV increase of 12%, AOV at target becomes ₹448, and the extra revenue at the same order volume is ₹48 × 1,600 = ₹76,800 a month, or ₹9,21,600 over a year if order volume holds.

Tie the ₹48 to one specific action. If staff suggest a ₹120 dessert and 40% of bills add one, that is 640 desserts and exactly ₹76,800 of extra sales. The figure is revenue, not profit: at an ingredient cost of ₹36 per dessert, the extra [gross profit](/glossary/gross-profit) is 640 × ₹84 = ₹53,760. Set your target percentage from a concrete [upselling](/glossary/upselling) plan like this rather than a guess.

guide.headline: Reading your AOV correctly
items: Watch order count alongside AOV. The extra revenue figure assumes orders stay the same; if AOV rises but orders fall, total sales may not grow.
Split by channel. Delivery app orders, takeaway and dine-in usually have very different AOVs, and a blended number hides changes in the mix.
Compare like with like. Weekends and festival weeks can run a higher AOV, so compare the same days or weeks before and after a change.
Leave out one-off bulk orders such as catering or corporate lunches, which can make a normal month's AOV look higher than it is.
Watch the discount behind a combo. A bundle that lifts AOV by selling items at a deep discount can raise revenue per bill while lowering profit per bill.

hero.headline: Menu Engineering Calculator

about.headline: Stop guessing which items drive profit
paragraphs: Menu engineering is the practice of analyzing your menu items by contribution margin and popularity to identify which items are genuinely profitable and which are eating into your margins.

This tool classifies every item into one of four categories: Stars (high profit, high popularity) that should be promoted, Cash Cows (high profit, low popularity) that need visibility, Puzzles (low profit, high popularity) that need repricing, and Dogs (low profit, low popularity) that should be removed or repositioned. Input your menu items with their prices, costs and units sold — the calculator handles the rest.

items.question: What does 'contribution margin' mean in menu engineering?
items.answer: Contribution margin is the profit per item before allocating fixed overhead costs (rent, salaries, etc.). It's the amount each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and generating profit, calculated as Selling Price minus Cost of Goods Sold.

items.question: How are items classified in menu engineering?
items.answer: Items are classified by comparing their contribution margin and popularity (units sold) against the menu average. Stars are high on both, Cash Cows are high margin but low popularity, Puzzles are high popularity but low margin, and Dogs are low on both.

items.question: What should I do with each classification?
items.answer: Stars — promote heavily, keep pricing stable. Cash Cows — increase visibility and bundling to boost sales. Puzzles — increase price or reduce costs (they're already popular, just not profitable). Dogs — remove, reposition as a loss-leader, or improve the recipe cost.

items.question: Does popularity mean units sold or revenue?
items.answer: In this calculator, popularity means units or covers sold, not revenue. A low-margin item that sells in high volume is a Puzzle, not a Star, because it ties up kitchen capacity without delivering margin.

items.question: How often should I re-run this analysis?
items.answer: At least once a month or whenever you introduce new items or make significant price or recipe changes. Seasonal changes in popularity often shift items between categories, so you can spot shifting dynamics and adjust positioning.

items.question: Does this account for labour cost?
items.answer: No — this calculator uses ingredient cost only to find contribution margin. For a more complete profit picture, add an estimated labour cost per item (prep time, cooking time, plating) to your COGS before calculating margin.

items.question: Can I download the menu engineering report as Excel or PDF?
items.answer: Yes. Export to Excel saves a file named menu-engineering-report.xlsx with each item's name, price, cost, margin, margin %, units sold and classification. Export to PDF saves a landscape A4 report with the date, total revenue, total cost, total contribution, average margin, the number of items in each category and the full item table. Both files are created in your browser.

items.question: How is this calculator different from the classic Kasavana-Smith menu engineering matrix?
items.answer: The classic method compares each dish's rupee contribution margin with the menu's weighted average and treats a dish as popular if its share of sales is at least 70% of an equal share. This calculator compares margin % with the simple average and units sold with the average units, so the same menu can sort differently. Labels differ too: a popular, low-margin dish is a Puzzle here but a Plowhorse in the classic matrix.

items.question: Is Avg Margin % weighted by units sold?
items.answer: No. Avg Margin % is a simple average of each dish's margin %, so every item counts once however many plates it sold. For your overall margin, divide Total Contribution by Total Revenue. With chai at ₹40 (₹10 cost, 500 sold) and a thali at ₹200 (₹100 cost, 50 sold), Avg Margin % shows 62.5%, while the sales-weighted margin is ₹20,000 ÷ ₹30,000 = 66.7%.

items.question: Does the menu engineering calculator save my menu items?
items.answer: No. Items stay only while the page is open; refreshing or closing the tab brings back the four sample dishes. To keep your analysis, use Export to Excel or Export to PDF before you leave. The exported file cannot be loaded back into the calculator, so keep your item list handy to re-enter for next month's run.

cta.headline: Optimize your menu with real-time data
cta.subtext: Setu Dine tracks every item's cost and sales automatically, so you can run menu engineering analysis daily and spot profit-killing items before they hurt your bottom line.

guide.headline: Menu engineering formulas
guide.text: [Contribution margin](/glossary/contribution-margin) = Price − Cost. Margin % = (Price − Cost) ÷ Price × 100. Average margin % = simple average of every item's margin %, and average popularity = simple average of Units Sold. An item is high margin if its margin % is at or above the average, and high popularity if its units sold are at or above the average. Star = high margin and high popularity; Cash Cow = high margin, low popularity; Puzzle = low margin, high popularity; Dog = low on both. Total revenue = sum of Price × Units Sold. Total cost = sum of Cost × Units Sold. Total contribution = Total revenue − Total cost.

guide.headline: How to use the menu engineering calculator
steps: Delete the four sample dishes with the bin icon, or type over them with your own.
For each dish, enter the Item Name, its menu Price and its Cost, the ingredient cost of one plate.
Enter Units Sold for every dish from the same period, such as last month's sales report. Units must be whole numbers.
Tap Add Menu Item for each extra dish you want in the analysis.

Read the summary cards (Total Revenue, Total Cost, Total Contribution, Avg Margin %) and the count of Stars, Cash Cows, Puzzles and Dogs. Then check each dish's margin, margin % and badge in the results table, which is sorted by units sold.
Click Export to Excel or Export to PDF to save the analysis.

guide.headline: Worked example: five dishes from one month of sales
paragraphs: Take five dishes and a month of sales: Veg Thali (₹200 price, ₹70 cost, 300 sold), Paneer Butter Masala (₹260, ₹78, 220), Chicken Biryani (₹320, ₹128, 250), Mushroom Tikka (₹240, ₹60, 90) and Fish Curry (₹380, ₹190, 60). Their margins are 65%, 70%, 60%, 75% and 50%, so the average margin is 320 ÷ 5 = 64%, and average units sold is 920 ÷ 5 = 184. The menu engineering calculator marks Veg Thali and Paneer Butter Masala as Stars, Chicken Biryani as a Puzzle, Mushroom Tikka as a Cash Cow and Fish Curry as a Dog. Total revenue is ₹2,41,600, total cost ₹86,960 and total contribution ₹1,54,640.

The Puzzle label does not make Chicken Biryani a weak dish. Its ₹192 margin across 250 plates is ₹48,000 of contribution, the most on the menu; it lands in Puzzle only because its 60% margin is below the 64% average. A ₹20 price rise would add ₹5,000 a month if volume holds at 250 plates. Fish Curry, the Dog, still earns ₹190 a plate, the second-highest rupee margin on the list, but spends half its price on ingredients and sold only 60 plates. Rework its cost in the [recipe costing calculator](/calculators/recipe-costing-calculator) or give it better menu placement before you decide to remove it.

guide.headline: Getting reliable menu engineering results
items: Pull units sold for every dish from the same period of sales data, such as the last 30 days.
Analyse one menu section at a time. A ₹40 chai can outsell every main course and pull the popularity average up for the whole list.
Use a costed plate figure for Cost, not a guess. A ₹10 error on a ₹200 dish moves its margin by 5 points and can change its category.
Leave out dishes that were added or unavailable for part of the period, since fewer selling days make them look less popular than they are.
Before dropping a Dog or repricing a Puzzle, multiply its rupee Margin by Units Sold to see the contribution it brings in. The categories here are set by margin %, not rupee margin.
Export to Excel each month and keep the files, so you can see which dishes move between categories.

about.headline: Why use a VAT calculator
paragraphs: If you sell to customers or buy from suppliers in countries that use VAT — the UK, EU, UAE, South Africa and 170+ others — you constantly need to move between net and gross prices. Doing it by hand is error-prone, especially with rates like 12.5% or 23%.

This calculator works both directions. Enter a net amount to see the VAT and gross total, or enter a VAT-inclusive price to recover the net amount and the tax inside it. Quick-select buttons cover the most common rates worldwide, and you can type any custom rate.

items.question: How do I add VAT to a price?
items.answer: Multiply the net price by the VAT rate and add it on. At 20% VAT, a 100 net price carries 20 of VAT for a 120 gross total. This calculator does it instantly for any rate.

items.question: How do I remove VAT from a gross amount?
items.answer: Divide the gross amount by (1 + rate). A 120 gross price at 20% VAT is 120 ÷ 1.20 = 100 net, with 20 of VAT. Never subtract the percentage directly — that gives the wrong answer.

items.question: What's the difference between VAT and GST?
items.answer: They work the same way — a tax on the value added at each stage. Different countries just use different names and rates. India uses GST (use our GST calculator for CGST/SGST splits); the UK, EU and many others use VAT.

items.question: Which VAT rate should I use?
items.answer: Use the standard rate of the country where the sale is taxed — for example 20% in the UK, 19% in Germany, 5% in the UAE. Many countries also have reduced rates for essentials; check the category of your goods or services.

items.question: Which countries are in the VAT calculator's rate table?
items.answer: The table holds standard rates for more than 60 countries, including the United Kingdom at 20%, Germany at 19%, Saudi Arabia at 15% and the UAE at 5%. Countries that call the tax GST, such as Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Canada, carry a GST label. Search by country name or two-letter code to find a row, and tick Use a custom rate for any country that is not listed.

items.question: Can I calculate a reduced or zero VAT rate?
items.answer: Yes. Tick Use a custom rate and type any rate, such as 5% for a UK reduced-rate item or 7% for Germany's reduced rate. For many countries the table also shows the reduced rates as a reminder, in the notes column on wider screens and under the selected rate. Enter 0 for a zero-rated item and the VAT amount shows as zero.

items.question: Can the VAT calculator show euros, pounds or dirhams instead of rupees?
items.answer: Yes. Money on Setu's calculators is shown in the currency saved in the free Business Profile tool, which is Indian rupees until you change it. Pick euro, pound, dirham or any other currency there and the VAT calculator follows in the same browser. The VAT arithmetic is identical in every currency, so you can also leave it in rupees and read the numbers as your invoice currency.

items.question: Do Indian exporters have to charge VAT to overseas customers?
items.answer: Usually not. Exports of goods and services from India are treated as zero-rated supplies under GST, and any VAT on imported goods is normally paid by the importer in the buyer's country. You charge foreign VAT yourself only if you are registered for VAT there, for example when selling from stock held in that country. Digital services sold to overseas consumers can follow different rules, so check with an adviser.

guide.headline: VAT formula
guide.text: Add VAT: VAT = Net amount × Rate ÷ 100, and Gross amount = Net amount + VAT. Remove VAT: Net amount = Gross amount ÷ (1 + Rate ÷ 100), and VAT = Gross amount − Net amount. The rate is the standard rate of the country you pick in the table, or your own figure when **Use a custom rate** is ticked.

Search the country table by name or two-letter code, such as AE or GB, and tap the row to load its standard rate.

Enter the figure in Amount before VAT or Amount including VAT, depending on the mode.

guide.headline: Worked example: VAT on a UAE quote and a London hotel bill
paragraphs: A Dubai supplier quotes AED 8,000 plus [VAT](/glossary/vat) for a commercial oven for your new outlet there. In the VAT calculator, choose Add VAT, pick the United Arab Emirates at 5% and enter 8,000. VAT = 8,000 × 5 ÷ 100 = 400, so the gross amount you pay is **AED 8,400**.

Going the other way, a London hotel bill for a trade fair comes to £1,500 including 20% VAT. Choose Remove VAT, pick the United Kingdom and enter 1,500. Net = 1,500 ÷ 1.20 = £1,250, and VAT = 1,500 − 1,250 = **£250**. Taking 20% of £1,500 instead would give £300 of VAT and a wrong net of £1,200, overstating the tax by £50. Whatever currency the invoice is in, the arithmetic is the same.

guide.headline: VAT tips for Indian businesses dealing abroad
items: Check whether a foreign quote is net or gross. Business quotes in the UK and EU are usually net of VAT, while prices shown to consumers usually include it.
To check a VAT-inclusive figure in your head, the VAT is rate ÷ (100 + rate) of the gross: one-sixth at 20% and one twenty-first at 5%.
If you invoice from a VAT registration abroad, show the net amount, VAT rate and VAT amount as separate lines, as VAT invoices generally require.
For sales inside India, charge GST rather than VAT: split it into CGST and SGST for a sale within your state, or charge IGST for an interstate sale.
Record the VAT on a foreign supplier's invoice separately from the cost in your books; whether a foreign business can reclaim it depends on that country's rules.
Rates change with national budgets, so confirm the current rate on the tax authority's website before invoicing a large amount.

about.headline: How US sales tax works
paragraphs: Unlike VAT or GST, US sales tax is added at the register and varies by state, county and city. The rate you charge is usually the state rate plus any local rates that apply at the point of sale — which is why two shops a few miles apart can charge different tax.

Enter the state rate and any local/city rate, and this calculator shows the combined rate, the tax amount and the total. Flip it around to extract the tax from a receipt total when you're doing your books or claiming expenses.

items.question: How do I calculate sales tax on a purchase?
items.answer: Multiply the pre-tax price by the combined tax rate. A $100 purchase at a combined 8% rate carries $8 of tax for a $108 total.

items.question: How do I work out the pre-tax price from a total?
items.answer: Divide the total by (1 + combined rate). A $108 total at 8% is $108 ÷ 1.08 = $100 pre-tax and $8 of tax.

items.question: Why do I need separate state and local rates?
items.answer: Most US states let counties, cities and special districts add their own sales tax on top of the state rate. The rate the customer pays is the combined total at the sale location, so this calculator takes both and adds them for you.

items.question: Do all US states charge sales tax?
items.answer: No — Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon have no state-wide sales tax (though some Alaska localities charge their own). Every other state has a state rate, typically between 4% and 7.25%.

items.question: Why does the sales tax calculator show ₹ instead of $?
items.answer: Money on Setu's calculators is shown in the currency saved in the Business Profile tool, which starts as Indian rupees. Change it to US dollar there and the sales tax calculator shows $ in the same browser. The calculation does not depend on the currency, so a result of ₹20.50 with rupees selected means $20.50 of tax on a dollar price.

items.question: How accurate are the local rates in the state table?
items.answer: The local column is a population-weighted average of the county, city and district rates across each state, so it suits estimates and comparisons between states. The actual rate at a particular address can be higher or lower than that average. For an invoice or a refund claim, take the exact rate from the receipt or the state tax department and enter it as a custom rate.

items.question: What is the difference between sales tax and VAT?
items.answer: US sales tax is charged once, when goods are sold to the final buyer, and businesses buying stock for resale generally do not pay it. VAT, like India's GST, is charged at every stage of the supply chain, and each registered business claims credit for the tax it paid on its purchases. The customer bears the tax either way, but the collection works differently.

items.question: Can I use a rate that is not in the table?

guide.text: Rate = State rate (State only), or State rate + Average local rate (Combined), or your own figure when **Use a custom rate** is ticked. For an exact city or county rate, tick Use a custom rate and enter it in Custom combined rate.
Enter the Pre-tax price or Total paid, then read the Pre-tax price, Sales tax and Total price.

guide.headline: Worked example: sales tax on a $250 order in Texas
paragraphs: Take a $250 sale taxed in Texas. In the sales tax calculator, choose Add tax to price and Combined, then pick Texas: the 6.25% state rate plus a 1.95% average local rate gives 8.20%. [Sales tax](/glossary/sales-tax) = 250 × 8.20 ÷ 100 = $20.50, so the total price is **$270.50**. Switch to State only and the tax at 6.25% comes to $15.63, for a total of $265.63.

To back the tax out of a receipt, choose Extract from total. A New York City receipt shows $435.50 paid at 8.875%. Tick Use a custom rate, enter 8.875 and the total: pre-tax price = 435.50 ÷ 1.08875 = $400.00, and sales tax = **$35.50**. Using the New York row instead, at its 8.53% combined average, would give $401.27 and $34.23, which is why the exact rate on the receipt beats the state average.

guide.headline: Sales tax tips for sellers
items: Record the state and rate used on each invoice, so a customer query or a state audit can be answered from your own files.
Keep the sales tax you collect out of revenue in your books, since it is owed to the state and is not income.
If you sell through a marketplace, check your payout report before adding tax, because large marketplaces usually collect and remit sales tax for their sellers.
Shipping and handling charges are taxable in some states and not in others, so check the state's rule before adding tax to delivery.
Many states exempt groceries and prescription medicines or tax them at a lower rate, so check the item before applying the general rate.

hero.headline: ROI Calculator

about.headline: Why ROI matters for every business decision
paragraphs: Whether it's new kitchen equipment, a marketing campaign, or stock for the season, every rupee you deploy should earn its keep. ROI puts all of those choices on one scale: what did the money return relative to what it cost?

The plain ROI percentage tells you the total gain. The annualized figure matters when comparing options with different timelines — a 40% return over 4 years is much weaker than 25% in one year. Enter the holding period and this calculator computes both.

items.question: How is ROI calculated?
items.answer: ROI = (amount returned − amount invested) ÷ amount invested × 100. Invest ₹1,00,000 and get back ₹1,40,000, and your ROI is 40%.

items.question: What is annualized ROI?
items.answer: It converts a total return into a per-year compound rate: (returned ÷ invested)^(1 ÷ years) − 1. A 40% total return over 2 years is about 18.3% per year — useful for comparing investments of different lengths.

items.question: What is a good ROI for a small business?
items.answer: It depends on the risk and your alternatives. As a rough bar, an investment should beat what the same money could earn safely (bank FD rates) by a wide enough margin to justify the effort and risk — many small-business owners look for 15–30%+ annually on operational investments.

items.question: Does this include ongoing costs?
items.answer: Include them in the invested amount, or subtract them from the returned amount — either way, ROI is only as honest as the numbers you feed it. For marketing, our CAC calculator complements this by tracking cost per customer.

items.question: What is the difference between ROI and payback period?
items.answer: ROI tells you how much an investment earned in total compared with what it cost. Payback period tells you how long it takes for the money coming back to equal the money you spent. A machine can have a high ROI but a long payback, which matters when cash is tight. This calculator gives total and annualized ROI. For a rough payback figure, divide the cost by the cash the investment brings in each year, if that cash is fairly even.

items.question: Can I use the ROI calculator for a period shorter than one year?
items.answer: Yes. Enter the holding period as a decimal, such as 0.5 for six months or 0.25 for three months. For a gain, the annualized ROI will then be higher than the total ROI, because it assumes you could repeat the same return, compounded, for a full year. A loss looks worse once annualized. Use the figure to compare options, not as a promised yearly return.

items.question: What does a negative ROI mean?
items.answer: It means you got back less than you put in. The first result switches to Net loss and the ROI shows as a negative percentage. For example, investing ₹1,00,000 and getting back ₹85,000 gives a net loss of ₹15,000 and an ROI of −15%. A negative figure early in an investment is not always final, so check whether returns are still coming in.

items.question: Is ROI the same as profit margin?
items.answer: No. ROI compares profit with the money you invested, while profit margin compares profit with your sales. Say a shop spends ₹50,000 on a display fridge, and over the fridge's life the extra drinks it sells bring back ₹70,000 after the cost of the drinks. The ROI is 40%, because (70,000 − 50,000) ÷ 50,000 = 0.4, whatever margin the shop makes on each bottle. Use ROI to judge spending and margin to judge pricing.

guide.headline: ROI formula
guide.text: Net profit = Amount returned − Amount invested. ROI % = (Amount returned − Amount invested) ÷ Amount invested × 100. Annualized ROI % = ((Amount returned ÷ Amount invested)^(1 ÷ Holding period in years) − 1) × 100. The annualized figure is shown only when the holding period is above zero.

guide.headline: How to use the ROI calculator
steps: Enter the amount invested: the full cost of the machine, campaign, renovation or stock you are judging.
Enter the amount returned: the total money that came back, not just the gain. If you put in ₹1,00,000 and earned ₹30,000 on top, enter ₹1,30,000.
Enter the holding period in years to get the annualized figure. Use decimals for part-years, such as 0.5 for six months, or clear the field if you only need total ROI.
Read the net profit (labelled net loss if you got back less than you put in), the ROI % and the annualized ROI %. All three update as you type.
Change one figure at a time to compare options, such as a cheaper machine that returns less, or the same spend over a shorter period.

guide.headline: Worked example: a ₹2,00,000 coffee machine over 3 years
paragraphs: A café buys an espresso machine for ₹2,00,000. Over three years the extra coffee sales add ₹2,40,000 of profit after beans, milk and staff time, and the machine can be sold for ₹50,000 at the end, so ₹2,90,000 comes back in total. Enter ₹2,00,000 as invested, ₹2,90,000 as returned and 3 years as the holding period. The ROI calculator shows a net profit of ₹90,000, an ROI of 45% and an annualized ROI of 13.19%. That is lower than 45 ÷ 3 = 15% because the yearly rate compounds: 1.1319 × 1.1319 × 1.1319 ≈ 1.45.

Now compare ₹50,000 of extra festive stock that brings in ₹60,000 within six months. With a holding period of 0.5 years, ROI is 20% but annualized ROI is 44%, since 1.20 × 1.20 = 1.44. Per year the stock looks far better, but only if you can repeat that turnaround twice a year. For projects where cash arrives unevenly over many years, also look at the [payback period](/glossary/payback-period) and [net present value](/glossary/net-present-value).

guide.headline: Tips for an honest ROI figure
items: Enter the total amount returned, including the cost you recovered, not just the net gain. Typing only the gain can make a good investment look like a loss.
Use profit, not sales, as the return. ₹1,00,000 of extra sales at a 30% gross margin brings back only ₹30,000.
Count one-time costs that are easy to forget, such as delivery, installation, staff training and any GST you cannot claim back as input tax credit.
Compare options on annualized ROI when their timelines differ, and on total ROI only when they run for the same period.
Work out ROI twice, once with a cautious return and once with your expected return, so you know how much room for error the decision has.

seo.description: Free depreciation calculator. Compute straight-line or written-down-value (declining balance) depreciation with a full year-by-year schedule of book values.

hero.headline: Depreciation Calculator
hero.subheadline: Enter the asset cost, salvage value and life — get the annual depreciation and a full year-by-year schedule, straight-line or WDV.

about.headline: Two methods, one schedule
paragraphs: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life, and the method changes the shape of the expense. Straight-line splits the cost evenly each year — simple and common for furniture, fittings and equipment. Written down value (declining balance) applies a fixed percentage to the remaining book value, front-loading the expense — the approach the Indian Income Tax Act uses for most asset blocks.

This calculator produces the full schedule for either method: opening value, depreciation and closing book value for every year, so you can drop the numbers straight into your accounts or compare methods before choosing.

items.question: How does straight-line depreciation work?
items.answer: Annual depreciation = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life. A ₹5,00,000 machine with ₹50,000 salvage over 5 years depreciates ₹90,000 per year.

items.question: How does written down value (WDV) work?
items.answer: Each year you depreciate a fixed percentage of the remaining book value. At 25% WDV, a ₹5,00,000 asset depreciates ₹1,25,000 in year one, then 25% of ₹3,75,000 in year two, and so on — bigger deductions early, smaller later.

items.question: Which method should I use?
items.answer: For Indian income-tax purposes, WDV at prescribed block rates is standard for most businesses. For your own management accounts, straight-line is simpler and shows a steady cost. Companies reporting under the Companies Act follow Schedule II useful lives. When in doubt, ask your CA/CPA.

items.question: What is salvage (residual) value?
items.answer: The amount you expect the asset to be worth at the end of its useful life — resale or scrap value. Depreciation stops once the book value reaches it.

items.question: Can I calculate depreciation for part of a year or by month?
items.answer: The calculator works in whole years and rounds the useful life to the nearest year, up to 50. For a monthly figure under straight line, divide the annual depreciation by 12, so ₹46,666.67 a year is ₹3,888.89 a month. For an asset bought mid-year, multiply the first year's charge by the months it was in use and divide by 12, or follow the rule your CA/CPA applies for tax.

items.question: What is the difference between depreciation and amortisation?
items.answer: Depreciation spreads the cost of physical assets such as machinery, furniture, vehicles and computers. Amortisation does the same for intangible assets such as software licences, franchise fees or trademarks, usually in equal amounts over the asset's term. You can use the straight-line mode here to amortise an intangible by entering its cost, a salvage value of zero and the term in years.

items.question: Is depreciation a cash expense?
items.answer: No. You pay for the asset when you buy it, or through a loan, and depreciation only spreads that cost across later years in the profit and loss statement. It lowers reported profit, and tax depreciation lowers taxable profit, without any money leaving the bank that year. That is why it is added back to net profit when you prepare a cash flow statement using the indirect method.

items.question: What depreciation rate should I use for the WDV method?
items.answer: For income tax, use the rate prescribed for the asset's block. Rates long applied include 15% for general plant and machinery, 10% for furniture and fittings and 40% for computers, but confirm the current rate with your CA/CPA. For your own accounts, pick a rate that brings the book value close to the salvage value by the end of the asset's useful life.

guide.headline: Depreciation formulas
guide.text: Straight line: Annual depreciation = (Asset cost − Salvage value) ÷ Useful life, charged every year until the book value reaches the salvage value. Written down value: Depreciation for the year = Opening value × Rate ÷ 100, but never more than Opening value − Salvage value. For both methods, Closing value = Opening value − Depreciation, each year's closing value becomes the next year's opening value, and the schedule runs for the useful life you enter.

guide.headline: How to use the depreciation calculator
steps: Choose Straight line or Written down value at the top.
Enter the Asset cost and the Salvage value you expect at the end of the asset's life.
Enter the Useful life in years; the calculator rounds it to a whole number and runs up to 50 years.
For written down value, enter the Depreciation rate as a percentage.
Read the annual or first-year depreciation and the book value at end of life, then check the year-by-year table of opening value, depreciation and closing value.

guide.headline: Worked example: depreciating ₹1,50,000 of billing computers
paragraphs: A restaurant buys billing computers for ₹1,50,000 and expects to sell them for ₹10,000 after 3 years. With [straight-line depreciation](/glossary/straight-line-depreciation) the depreciation calculator charges (1,50,000 − 10,000) ÷ 3 = **₹46,666.67** each year, so the book value falls to ₹1,03,333.33, then ₹56,666.67, and ends at exactly ₹10,000.

Switch to [written down value](/glossary/written-down-value) at 40%, the rate long prescribed for computers in Indian income-tax rules. Year 1 depreciation is 40% of ₹1,50,000 = ₹60,000, leaving ₹90,000. Year 2 is 40% of ₹90,000 = ₹36,000, leaving ₹54,000. Year 3 is ₹21,600, leaving ₹32,400. WDV front-loads the expense, ₹60,000 against ₹46,666.67 in year one, but at this rate it does not reach the salvage value, so ₹32,400 is still on the books after three years.

guide.headline: Depreciation tips from accounting practice
items: Include freight, installation and other costs of getting the asset ready for use in the asset cost.
Leave GST out of the asset cost if you claim it as input tax credit; you cannot claim both the credit and depreciation on the same tax.
The calculator charges a full year in year one; for income tax, an asset put to use for less than 180 days in its first year generally gets only half the rate that year.
Tax depreciation is worked out on blocks of similar assets, not on each item, so use this schedule per asset for your fixed asset register and let your CA/CPA compute the tax block.
To make WDV finish on your salvage value, use a rate of (1 − (Salvage ÷ Cost)^(1 ÷ Life)) × 100; for ₹1,50,000 down to ₹10,000 over 3 years that is about 59.5%.
Land is never depreciated, while buildings, furniture, machinery, vehicles and computers are.

about.headline: Decode invoice terms in seconds
paragraphs: Terms like "net 30" or "2/10 net 45" pack a due date, a discount and an implicit interest rate into a few characters. This calculator unpacks them: the exact calendar due date from the invoice date, the discount amount if you pay within the window, and the annualized cost of choosing not to.

That last number surprises people. Skipping a 2% discount to hold cash for 20 extra days is equivalent to borrowing at over 36% per year — far more expensive than most working-capital finance. Knowing that lets you decide with numbers, whether you're the buyer or the seller setting terms.

items.question: What does 2/10 net 30 mean?
items.answer: Pay within 10 days and take a 2% discount off the invoice; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days from the invoice date.

items.question: How is the cost of skipping a discount calculated?
items.answer: Cost ≈ (discount % ÷ (100 − discount %)) × (365 ÷ extra days of credit) × 100. For 2/10 net 30, that's (2 ÷ 98) × (365 ÷ 20) ≈ 37% per year — what the extra 20 days of credit effectively costs.

items.question: Is the due date counted from the invoice date or delivery date?
items.answer: Usually the invoice date, unless the contract says otherwise (some use end-of-month terms, written "net 30 EOM"). This calculator counts calendar days from the invoice date you enter.

items.question: Should I offer early-payment discounts to my customers?
items.answer: If cash flow is tight or debtors pay slowly, a small discount can pull cash in dramatically faster and cut follow-up effort. Price it consciously — the same annualized-cost math applies to you as the seller.

items.question: Does the due date skip Sundays and bank holidays?
items.answer: No. The calculator counts plain calendar days from the invoice date, so a net 30 due date can land on a Sunday or a public holiday. If your contract does not say how such dates are handled, pay on the previous working day so the payment is not late, or agree the rule with your supplier in writing.

items.question: Is the early payment discount worked out before or after GST?
items.answer: The calculator applies the discount percentage to whatever invoice amount you enter. Enter the total bill if the supplier allows the discount on the full amount, or the taxable value if the terms say so. Whether the discount also reduces the GST depends on how it was agreed and documented, usually through a credit note, so confirm the treatment with your accountant.

items.question: What is the difference between due on receipt and net 30?
items.answer: Due on receipt means the customer should pay as soon as the invoice arrives. Net 30 gives them 30 calendar days from the invoice date. To see a due-on-receipt invoice in this calculator, set the payment terms to 0 days and the due date will match the invoice date. Shorter terms bring cash in faster, but larger buyers often push for longer ones.

items.question: Does the calculator work out interest on late payments?
items.answer: No. It covers the due date, the early payment discount and the cost of skipping it. Late payment interest depends on what your contract or invoice says. If your supplier is a micro or small manufacturer or service provider registered under Udyam, the MSMED Act sets interest on delayed payments at three times the bank rate notified by the RBI, compounded monthly, whatever the contract says.

guide.text: Payment due date = Invoice date + Net days, counted in calendar days. Pay-early date = Invoice date + Discount window days. Early payment saving = Invoice amount × Discount % ÷ 100. Cost of skipping the discount (% per year) = Discount % ÷ (100 − Discount %) × 365 ÷ (Net days − Discount window days) × 100. When the discount window is as long as the net term or longer, the cost shows 0%.

Pick the invoice date. It starts on today's date, so change it for an older bill.
Type the payment terms in net days, or tap a preset: Net 7, 15, 30, 45, 60 or 90.

Read the payment due date. With a discount above 0 you also see the pay-early-by date, the rupee saving from paying early and the yearly cost of skipping the discount.

guide.headline: Worked example: 1/15 net 45 on a ₹2,50,000 invoice
paragraphs: A restaurant gets a ₹2,50,000 bill from its dry-goods supplier dated 15 October 2026, on terms of 1/15 net 45: 1% off if paid within 15 days, otherwise the full amount in 45 days. In the payment terms calculator, enter ₹2,50,000, the invoice date, 45 net days, a 1% discount and a 15-day window. It shows a payment due date of 29 Nov 2026, a pay-early date of 30 Oct 2026 and a saving of ₹2,500. Paying early therefore means sending ₹2,47,500 instead of ₹2,50,000.

Skipping the discount buys 30 extra days of credit (45 − 15) for ₹2,500. The calculator annualizes that as 1 ÷ 99 × 365 ÷ 30 × 100 = 12.3% a year. If your overdraft or cash credit limit costs less than that and has room, paying early with borrowed money comes out cheaper. If it costs more, holding the cash until day 45 is the better use of your [working capital](/glossary/working-capital). For plain terms without a discount, see how [net 30](/glossary/net-30) works.

guide.headline: Payment terms tips for buyers and sellers
items: Write terms in words on every invoice, such as "1% off if paid within 15 days, otherwise due in 45 days", so the customer's accounts team cannot misread them.
Agree terms in the quotation or purchase order before the goods ship, so the invoice only repeats what both sides already accepted.
If there is no early payment discount, pay on the due date rather than before it. Those days of credit cost you nothing.

Buying from a micro or small manufacturer or service provider registered under Udyam? The MSMED Act caps agreed credit at 45 days (15 days if nothing was agreed), and paying later can delay your income tax deduction for that expense until the year you actually pay.
Pay suppliers within 180 days of the invoice date. Under GST rules, input tax credit on bills still unpaid after 180 days has to be reversed, and can be claimed again once you pay.
Track open invoices by age so that bills past 30, 60 and 90 days get followed up before they turn into bad debts.

about.headline: Catch cost creep before it eats your margin
paragraphs: Purchase price variance measures the gap between what you planned to pay for materials or stock and what you actually paid. Suppliers raise rates quietly, order sizes change, market prices move — PPV is how buying teams spot it early and quantify the impact.

A positive (unfavourable) variance means purchases cost more than the standard — margin is leaking on the way in. A negative (favourable) variance means you beat the plan. Track it per item and per supplier, and feed persistent variances back into your pricing or renegotiation.

items.question: How is purchase price variance calculated?
items.answer: PPV = (actual price − standard price) × quantity purchased. Buying 500 units at ₹110 against a ₹100 standard gives an unfavourable variance of ₹5,000.

items.question: What is the standard price?
items.answer: The benchmark you planned around — a budgeted rate, a negotiated contract price, or last period's average cost. Consistency matters more than which one you choose.

items.question: Is a favourable variance always good?
items.answer: Usually, but check why. A cheaper price from lower quality, bigger-than-needed bulk orders, or missed delivery windows can cost more downstream than the variance saves.

items.question: How often should I review PPV?
items.answer: Monthly works for most small businesses — often enough to catch supplier increases before they compound, without drowning in noise. Review your highest-spend items first (our ABC analysis tool helps rank them).

items.question: Can I calculate purchase price variance for several items at once?
items.answer: Yes. Each row is one item, with its own standard cost, actual cost and quantity. Add as many rows as you need with the add item button. The calculator totals the variance across all of them and counts the items compared. When an item cost more than standard, it names the biggest overrun. When one cost less, it names the biggest saving.

items.question: Why is an item not included in the total variance?
items.answer: A row counts only when it has an item name and a quantity above zero. If you enter prices but leave the name blank or the quantity empty, the variance impact shows a dash. The row is then left out of the total and the items compared count. Fill in both and the row is added straight away.

items.question: Should purchase price variance include GST?
items.answer: If you claim input tax credit on the purchase, compare prices without GST, because you get the tax back and it is not part of your cost. If you cannot claim it, for example under the composition scheme, the GST is a real cost and you can include it. Either way, keep standard and actual prices on the same basis.

items.question: What is the difference between purchase price variance and budget variance?
items.answer: Purchase price variance looks only at price: how much more or less you paid per unit, multiplied by the quantity you actually bought. Budget variance compares total actual spend with the total budget, so it mixes price changes with buying more or less than planned. A budget overrun can come entirely from buying more, even when the price variance is zero.

guide.headline: Purchase price variance formula
guide.text: **Variance impact = (Actual cost − Standard cost) × Qty**, worked out for each row. Total variance = the sum of the variance impacts of every row that has an item name and a quantity above zero. A positive total is unfavourable and a negative one is favourable. The percentage shown for the biggest overrun = (Actual cost − Standard cost) ÷ Standard cost × 100. See [purchase price variance](/glossary/purchase-price-variance) for the term.

guide.headline: Worked example: purchase price variance at a sweet shop
paragraphs: A sweet shop compares three items bought this month against its standard rates. Ghee: standard ₹560 per kg, actual ₹590, 80 kg bought, so (₹590 − ₹560) × 80 = ₹2,400 unfavourable. Sugar: standard ₹44 per kg, actual ₹42, 500 kg, so (₹42 − ₹44) × 500 = −₹1,000, a favourable variance. Khoya: standard ₹300 per kg, actual ₹320, 60 kg, so ₹20 × 60 = ₹1,200 unfavourable. Total variance is ₹2,400 − ₹1,000 + ₹1,200 = ₹2,600 unfavourable.

The calculator names ghee as the biggest overrun: ₹2,400 above plan, 5.4% per unit. Khoya's price rose faster, by 6.7% per unit, but the quantity was smaller, so it cost less in rupees. Ghee is the first supplier to talk to. Sugar shows as the biggest saving, ₹1,000 below plan. Check its quality and pack size before you count on that saving.

guide.headline: Getting a PPV figure you can act on
items: Use the same unit for standard and actual cost: per kg against per kg, not per kg against a 25 kg bag.
Compare on the same tax basis. If you claim input tax credit, leave GST out of both prices.
Treat freight and loading the same way in both prices: include them in both as landed cost, or leave them out of both.
Fix standard prices for a set period, such as a quarter or a financial year. Resetting them after every bill makes the variance disappear.
Act on rupee impact, not just percentage. A small rise on a high-volume item usually costs more than a big rise on a minor one.
