about.headline: A health check-up for your business
paragraphs: Individual numbers on a balance sheet say little on their own — ratios put them in context. Can you cover near-term bills (current and quick ratios)? Are you over-borrowed (debt to equity)? Is the core trade profitable (gross and net margins)? Is cash stuck in stock or with customers (inventory turnover and receivable days)?

Banks and investors compute exactly these ratios when they look at your accounts, so it pays to see them first. Enter the figures from your latest balance sheet and P&L — or build those statements with our free Balance Sheet and P&L tools — and read the results with the benchmarks provided.

items.question: What is a good current ratio?
items.answer: Between 1.5 and 3 is comfortable for most businesses. Below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets — a liquidity warning. Far above 3 may mean idle cash or overstocked inventory.

items.question: Why exclude inventory in the quick ratio?
items.answer: Stock can take months to turn into cash and may sell below book value under pressure. The quick ratio ((current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities) tests whether you could pay near-term bills without relying on selling stock.

items.question: What does debt-to-equity tell me?
items.answer: How much of the business is financed by borrowing versus the owners' money. Under 1 is conservative, 1–2 is common; above 2 means lenders carry more of the risk and new credit gets harder and pricier.

items.question: What are receivable days (DSO)?
items.answer: Accounts receivable ÷ annual revenue × 365 — the average number of days customers take to pay. If your payment terms are 30 days but DSO is 55, collections need attention (our Invoice Aging tool shows exactly where).

items.question: Where do I find these figures in a Tally balance sheet?
items.answer: In Tally, Current Assets and Current Liabilities are standard groups. Inventory is Stock-in-Hand and receivables are Sundry Debtors, both inside Current Assets. Total debt is usually the Loans (Liability) group, which holds Bank OD and secured or unsecured loans. Tally keeps Bank OD outside Current Liabilities, so decide whether to add it there and do the same every year. Owner's equity is the Capital Account plus the Profit & Loss A/c balance. Revenue, cost of goods sold and net profit come from the same year's P&L.

items.question: Can I use this for a proprietorship or partnership firm?
items.answer: Yes. The ratios work the same way for a proprietorship, partnership, LLP or company. For owner's equity, a proprietor uses the closing capital account balance after drawings and the year's profit; a partnership adds up all partners' capital accounts; a company uses share capital plus reserves and surplus. If the owner has lent money to the business separately, treat it the same way every year so the trend stays comparable.

items.question: What does an inventory turnover of 5 times mean?
items.answer: It means the cost of what you sold in the year was five times the stock you hold, so stock is replaced roughly every 73 days (365 ÷ 5). Fast-moving trades such as groceries usually turn stock more often than jewellery or furniture shops. If your suppliers give you 30 days' credit but stock takes 73 days to sell, you are funding about 43 days of stock from your own cash or borrowings.

items.question: Why is my quick ratio below 1 when my business is profitable?
items.answer: Profit and cash are different things. Profit may be tied up in stock and customer dues, or spent on loan repayments, equipment or the owner's drawings, so the money is not there to pay short-term bills. A quick ratio below 1 is common in stock-heavy trades such as retail and wholesale. What matters is whether it is steady or falling, and whether suppliers and the bank are being paid on time.

guide.headline: Financial ratio formulas
guide.text: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities. Quick ratio = (Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilities. Debt to equity = Total debt ÷ Owner's equity. Gross margin % = (Revenue − Cost of goods sold) ÷ Revenue × 100. Net margin % = Net profit ÷ Revenue × 100. Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold ÷ Inventory. Receivable days = Accounts receivable ÷ Revenue × 365.

guide.headline: How to use the financial ratio calculator
steps: Under balance sheet figures, enter current assets, inventory (stock), current liabilities and accounts receivable (sundry debtors).
Enter total debt, meaning term loans, overdraft and other borrowings, and owner's equity, meaning capital plus profit kept in the business.
Under P&L figures, enter a full year's revenue, cost of goods sold and net profit.
Read the seven results: current ratio, quick ratio, debt to equity, gross margin, net margin, inventory turnover and receivable days.
Compare each figure with last year's and with the rules of thumb shown below the results.

guide.headline: Worked example: a hardware wholesaler with ₹60 lakh sales
paragraphs: Take a hardware wholesaler with annual revenue of ₹60,00,000, cost of goods sold of ₹48,00,000 and net profit of ₹2,40,000. Its balance sheet shows current assets of ₹18,00,000, which include ₹9,00,000 of stock and ₹4,50,000 owed by customers, plus current liabilities of ₹12,00,000, total debt of ₹15,00,000 and owner's equity of ₹10,00,000. The financial ratio calculator gives a current ratio of 1.5 (18 ÷ 12), a quick ratio of 0.75 ((18 − 9) ÷ 12) and a debt to equity of 1.5 (15 ÷ 10).

Gross margin is 20% and net margin 4%. Inventory turnover is 5.3× (₹48 lakh ÷ ₹9 lakh), so stock sits for about 68 days on average, and receivable days come to 27 (4.5 ÷ 60 × 365). The weak spot is liquidity: without selling stock, the business can cover only 75 paise of each rupee it owes in the short term. Turning slow-moving stock into cash would lift the [quick ratio](/glossary/quick-ratio) without any new borrowing.

guide.headline: Getting ratios you can trust
items: Make sure the current assets figure already includes the stock and receivables you enter separately. The quick ratio subtracts inventory from that total.
Use full-year P&L figures. One quarter's revenue and cost of goods sold make receivable days four times too high and inventory turnover four times too low.
If stock or debtors swing with the season, a year-end balance can mislead. Run the calculator again with average opening and closing balances, and read turnover and receivable days from that run.
Take every figure from the same financial year's accounts, not a mix of final and provisional numbers.
Compare with your own previous years first. A ratio that slips year after year matters more than one figure against an industry average.

hero.headline: MDR Calculator
hero.subheadline: Work out the merchant discount rate on a payment, and what lands in your account once it and its GST come off.

about.headline: What MDR actually costs you
paragraphs: Merchant discount rate is the cut your acquirer keeps on every card or wallet collection, and GST is charged on that cut as well. On a ₹5,000 credit card sale at 2%, the MDR is ₹100 and the GST on it is another ₹18, so ₹4,882 settles rather than ₹5,000. Across a month of card volume that gap is real money, and most merchants only meet it in the settlement report.

Enter the amount two ways depending on what you know. MDR inclusive means the figure is what the customer pays, and the calculator tells you what you keep. MDR exclusive means the figure is what you want to land, and the calculator grosses the charge up so the net after MDR comes out exactly right — useful when you are recovering the charge from the customer or quoting a price that has to clear a fixed amount.

Not every rail costs the same, and UPI is about to change. From 15 October 2026, UPI merchant payments above ₹2,000 carry 0.4% MDR on the full amount, capped at ₹300 per transaction. At or below ₹2,000 there is still no MDR, RuPay debit and UPI Autopay mandates stay exempt, and merchants taking under ₹1 lakh a month by UPI QR are exempt as well — which is why collecting a large amount across several smaller QR codes can bring the cost to nothing.

items.question: What is MDR?
items.answer: MDR, or merchant discount rate, is the fee a merchant pays to accept a digital payment. It is usually a percentage of the transaction value, sometimes with a flat fee on top, and it is deducted before the money settles into the merchant's account. GST applies on the MDR itself.

items.question: What is the difference between MDR inclusive and MDR exclusive?
items.answer: MDR inclusive means the amount you entered is what the customer pays, and the MDR comes out of it, so you receive less. MDR exclusive means the amount you entered is what you want to receive, so the charge is grossed up to cover the MDR and its GST. Use exclusive when you need a specific figure to land in your account.

items.question: Is there MDR on UPI payments in India?
items.answer: Up to ₹2,000 there is none, and RuPay debit stays at zero by regulation. From 15 October 2026, UPI merchant payments above ₹2,000 attract 0.4% MDR, charged on the full transaction value and capped at ₹300. UPI Autopay and other recurring mandates are exempt, as are merchants receiving under ₹1 lakh a month through UPI QR.

items.question: How can I reduce what I pay in MDR?
items.answer: Steer customers toward the rails that stay free — UPI at or below ₹2,000, RuPay debit and UPI Autopay mandates — and negotiate your card rate with your acquirer once your volume justifies it. Because the ₹2,000 threshold is per transaction, keeping individual UPI collections under it avoids the 0.4% entirely; the linked QR splitter breaks a larger total into sub-threshold QR codes.

items.question: Is GST charged on MDR?
items.answer: Yes. GST at 18% is charged on the MDR itself, not on your sale or on the UPI transaction. The calculator shows it as a separate line so you can see the full cost of collection, and GST-registered businesses can generally claim it as input tax credit.

items.question: Which payment methods does the MDR calculator cover?
items.answer: The list has UPI merchant payments, UPI Autopay mandates, RuPay debit, UPI through a wallet, credit card on UPI, non-RuPay debit cards, credit cards, net banking and Amex or international cards, plus a custom option. Each fills in a typical rate, such as 0.9% for non-RuPay debit, 2% for credit cards and 1.8% for net banking. Treat these as starting points and overwrite them with the rate on your own agreement.

items.question: Why can MDR exclusive mode land a paisa more than I asked for?
items.answer: The exact gross-up rarely comes to whole paise: receiving ₹10,000 on a 2% card with 18% GST needs a charge of about ₹10,241.704. A charge has to be in whole paise, and the fee and its GST are each rounded to the paisa, so the calculator rounds the charge up rather than down. Here it charges ₹10,241.71 and ₹10,000.01 settles to you, so you never land below your target.

items.question: What does effective cost of collection mean?
items.answer: It is the total deducted, meaning the MDR plus the GST on it, as a percentage of what the customer paid. A 2% card rate works out to 2.36% once 18% GST is added. A flat per-transaction fee pushes the figure higher on small payments, and a capped payment method pushes it lower on large ones, which makes it a fairer number than the headline rate for comparing payment methods.

items.question: What happens if I change the rate on the UPI preset?
items.answer: The rate you type is used, but the UPI preset's ₹2,000 free threshold and ₹300 cap keep applying, because they belong to the payment method rather than the rate. That lets you test a different negotiated rate under the same rules. If you want a plain percentage with no threshold or cap, choose Custom rate from the payment method list and enter your own figure.

guide.headline: MDR formula
guide.text: MDR = Customer pays × MDR rate ÷ 100 + Flat fee. It is zero when the payment is at or below the payment method's free threshold, and it is held at the cap where the method has one. GST on MDR = MDR × GST rate ÷ 100. Total deducted = MDR + GST on MDR. You receive = Customer pays − Total deducted. Effective cost of collection = Total deducted ÷ Customer pays × 100. Each figure is rounded to the paisa. In **MDR exclusive** mode, Customer pays = (Target + Flat fee × (1 + GST ÷ 100)) ÷ (1 − MDR rate ÷ 100 × (1 + GST ÷ 100)), rounded up to the next paisa. Once the cap applies it is Target + Cap × (1 + GST ÷ 100), and it is simply the target when that sits at or below the free threshold; the calculator uses the lowest charge that delivers the target.

guide.headline: How to use the MDR calculator
steps: Under Amount you are entering, choose MDR inclusive if you know what the customer pays, or MDR exclusive if you know what you want to receive.
Type the figure in Amount customer pays or Amount you want to receive.
Pick the Payment method; a typical rate fills the MDR rate field, which you can overwrite with the rate on your acquirer agreement.
Leave GST on the MDR at 18% unless your acquirer's invoice shows otherwise, and enter any Flat fee per transaction your gateway charges.
Read Customer pays, You receive, MDR charged, GST on MDR, Total deducted and Effective cost of collection.
To collect a large amount by UPI without MDR, tap Split this into zero-MDR QR codes to open the splitter with the amount filled in.

guide.headline: Worked example: MDR on a ₹25,000 credit card payment
paragraphs: A clinic collects ₹25,000 for a procedure by credit card at a 2% MDR. In MDR inclusive mode the MDR calculator shows an MDR of ₹500 (25,000 × 2 ÷ 100), GST on MDR of ₹90 (500 × 18 ÷ 100) and a total deduction of ₹590. You receive **₹24,410**, and the effective cost of collection is 2.36%, not 2%, because the GST sits on top of the fee.

If the full ₹25,000 has to land, switch to MDR exclusive and enter 25,000. The charge becomes 25,000 ÷ (1 − 0.02 × 1.18) = 25,000 ÷ 0.9764, rounded up to **₹25,604.27**, with ₹512.09 of MDR and ₹92.18 of GST coming off. Simply adding 2% and charging ₹25,500 would still leave you ₹24,898.20. The same ₹25,000 paid through the UPI merchant preset at 0.4% costs ₹100 plus ₹18 of GST, so ₹24,882 reaches your [settlement](/glossary/settlement).

guide.headline: Practical checks on MDR
items: Compare the You receive figure with one line of your real settlement report; if they differ, your agreed rate or flat fee is not the preset.
Enter the flat fee if your gateway charges one: on a ₹200 debit card payment at 0.9% plus ₹3, the total deduction is ₹5.66, an effective 2.83%, against 1.13% on a ₹5,000 payment.
On the UPI merchant preset the MDR stops at ₹300, reached at ₹75,000, so the effective cost falls on bigger payments: 0.47% on ₹25,000 but ₹354 in all, or 0.35%, on ₹1,00,000.
Make sure your GSTIN is on record with your acquirer and keep the tax invoices it issues for MDR, so the GST you pay on the fee is available as input tax credit.
